articles.title: As Russian Arms Exports Slide, Central Asia Shops Elsewhere
articles.summary: Central Asian nations are increasingly turning to India, China, Turkey, and Europe for military equipment to reduce their dependence on Russia. Analysts note that this diversification offers greater political flexibility but could create long-term logistical and operational challenges.

articles.title: From Central Asia To Russia For Work -- And Into The Military
articles.summary: Kazakhstan has asked Moscow to help bring home citizens who say they were pressured into signing military contracts to fight in Ukraine. The request puts a fresh spotlight on the vulnerability of Central Asian migrants to Russia’s military enlistment efforts.

articles.title: Kyrgyz Activist Gets 2 Years For Criticizing Growing Chinese Presence
articles.summary: The Lenin District Court in Bishkek found activist and politician Mavlyan Askarbekov guilty and sentenced to two years in prison on offenses related to a law on incitement of racial, ethnic, national, religious, or interregional hatred, a verdict he called "absurd."

articles.title: Kyrgyzstan To Become Spacefaring Nation With Mini Satellite
articles.summary: Kyrgyzstan is set to send a domestically produced satellite into orbit on October 1, marking the Central Asian state's first feat of spacefaring. Uzbekistan has announced its own plans for a domestic satellite.

articles.title: 'Million Dollar' Mutton: Kyrgyzstan's New Monster Sheep Breed
articles.summary: A new Kyrgyz sheep breed is charging to fame in Central Asia for the size of its males and the massive prices being reported for prime specimens of the variety.

articles.title: Central Asia's Hijab Debate Flares Up As Schools Reopen
articles.summary: The hijab has long been a hot topic in Muslim-majority Central Asia, where many authoritarian governments have suppressed Islamic political and religious groups and any outward signs of religiosity. The debate has been rekindled as the new academic year started this month.

articles.title: In US-China AI Race, Kazakhstan Faces Pressure To Pick A Side
articles.summary: Kazakhstan is the only country to have joined both a US-led artificial intelligence initiative and a China-led rival. Now Washington is signaling that it may not be possible to sit on both sides of the emerging AI divide.

articles.title: Wider Europe Briefing: What To Expect At The EU's October Summit
articles.summary: In this week's briefing, RFE/RL Europe Editor Rikard Jozwiak drills down on one issue: the upcoming EU summit, with a focus on Ukraine, Russia sanctions, and EU enlargement.

articles.title: Germany To Start Nord Stream 'War Crime' Trial With Prosecutors Blaming Ukrainian 'State Authorities'
articles.summary: After four years of speculation, leaks, and briefings by anonymous sources, the world is finally about to hear evidence given publicly under oath in a German courtroom about how the Nord Stream gas pipelines were blown up -- in a case that could prove politically explosive.

articles.title: Latest Attack By Iran-Aligned Houthi Rebels On Saudi Airport Kills 1, Injures 11
articles.summary: As the conflict in the Persian Gulf continues to impact and shape the region, journalists from RFE/RL's Central Newsroom and Iranian service, Radio Farda, deliver ongoing updates and analysis.

articles.title: Zelenskyy Accuses Russia Of Breaking Trump's Cease-Fire On Energy Strikes
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump, in the face of sharp criticism from officials in Ukraine, Europe, and even his Republican party, defended his decision to allow Russian diesel exports and insisted an energy cease-fire between Kyiv and Moscow is in place despite a lack of confirmation from either side.

articles.title: Prominent Iranian Human Rights Lawyer Arrested
articles.summary: A prominent human rights lawyer and activist has been arrested in Iran, sources close to him told RFE/RL’s Radio Farda.

articles.title: Zelenskyy Says Yandex Strikes Crippled Pro-Kremlin Bots But Tech Experts Question Evidence
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that Ukraine's recent attacks on Russian tech giant Yandex’s data centers have resulted in fewer Internet bots promoting pro-Kremlin hate, a claim that has been disputed by many technology researchers.

articles.title: Zelenskyy Says Ukraine Will Stop Refinery Attacks If Russia Halts Energy Strikes
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia of striking an energy plant after US leader Donald Trump's surprise announcement of an “energy cease-fire,” while Moscow remained silent on any suggestion of a truce.

articles.title: House Republicans Move To Block Trump's Russia Diesel Deal
articles.summary: Republican Representative Brian Fitzpatrick plans to force a House vote on legislation blocking Russian oil purchases, challenging President Donald Trump's decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports as lawmakers warn the move could help finance Moscow's war against Ukraine.

articles.title: Trump Says Ukraine Should 'Get A New President' As Russia Kills At Least 20 In Air Strikes
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump blamed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for a stalemate in negotiations with Moscow, as Russian strikes on Ukraine killed at least 20 people, damaging apartment buildings and energy sites.

articles.title: Is Russia Preparing To Attack The Baltics?
articles.summary: Is Russia about to attack the Baltic states? There are no signs of an imminent conventional invasion, but concerns are growing that Moscow could test NATO in other ways.

articles.title: Why A Starlink Test In Italy Has Iran's Internet Censors Worried
articles.summary: A Starlink trial on an Italian hilltop connected an ordinary smartphone to the Internet without mobile coverage, a satellite dish, or an external antenna. It drew attention in Iran, where Internet access is heavily filtered and authorities imposed a near-total blackout during the January protests.

articles.title: Montenegro To Expel Head Of Russian Pro-War Blog Rybar
articles.summary: The head of a leading Russian pro-war blog linked to the country’s Defense Ministry has been detained in Montenegro, along with several other people who work for the blog.

articles.title: Impoverished Afghans Sell Kidneys On The Black Market 'Out Of Sheer Desperation'
articles.summary: Impoverished Afghans are illegally selling their kidneys to repay debts and buy food. The selling of organs comes as the war-torn country grapples with one of the world’s largest humanitarian crises.

articles.title: Too Soon? Swaths Of Chernobyl-Affected Land In Belarus To Lose 'Contaminated' Status
articles.summary: A recent announcement that 177 cities, towns and villages will lose their “contaminated” status on January 1, 2027 affects some 566,400 people from a total of 930,600 living on Belarusian territory that was contaminated by the 1986 nuclear accident in Soviet Ukraine.

articles.title: US, Ukraine Set For Talks In Miami Amid Onslaught Of Russian Air Strikes
articles.summary: The US and Ukraine will hold talks in Miami on October 9 to discuss proposals aimed at ending Russia’s war vital pieces of infrastructure in Kyiv and other citiies ahead of winter.

articles.title: Rubio Warns Russia's War Could Spill Beyond Ukraine's Borders
articles.summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned that Russia's war against Ukraine is at a stalemate but could escalate into a broader regional conflict if the deadlock pushes either side toward increasingly dangerous actions.

articles.title: More Drones, More Missiles, No Air Defenses: Moldova In The Cross Fire Of Russia's War On Ukraine
articles.summary: Moldova saw more Russian drones crash on its territory in August than it did over all of 2025. Moldovan authorities are increasingly rattled—but there’s little a cash-strapped government can do beyond complaining diplomatically.

articles.title: Dozens Killed In Russian Strike On Passenger Buses In Kramatorsk
articles.summary: Dozens of people were killed in a Russian strike on the Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk on October 8, according to local authorities, a day after another deadly barrage killed at least 25 people across Ukraine.

articles.title: No Safe Haven: How Iran And Russia Target Exile Enemies
articles.summary: Authoritarian states such as Russia and Iran are increasingly pursuing their opponents even after they find shelter in apparently safe Western countries. RFE/RL talks to some of those affected.

https://adcmemorial.org/en/news/witnesse.body: Facebook Twitter Вконтакте Elie Wiesel , a survivor of Auschwitz and Buchenwald and the author of the well-known autobiographical novel Night, wrote that “only those who experienced Auschwitz know what it was; the rest will never know.” As Wiesel saw it, “the witness knew then, as he knows now,” that his experience could not be conveyed or fully comprehended by those who had not been in a concentration camp and had not endured torture and humiliation. The author of the testimony asks: “Others will not know, but will they be able to understand?” And yet, despite his doubts, Wiesel “simply could not remain silent.” Reflecting on the destruction of European Jewry by the German Nazis, Wiesel concludes that over the years not only the actions but also the aims of the antisemites changed: if at the beginning of their rule the Nazis set themselves the task of “building a society without Jews,” towards the end they wanted “to leave behind a world in which Jews seemed never to have existed at all.” Violence against people — Jewish men, women and children — was accompanied by the destruction of the very memory of this people, their culture, language and religion. For many witnesses, the struggle against the destruction of memory became the purpose of their lives, an act of resistance. Contemporary antifascists often repeat that “to remember means to resist,” holding events in memory of comrades killed by neo-Nazis. “Memory Is Resistance” is the slogan on the website of members of Memorial who study the history of political repression in the USSR and preserve testimonies of the horrors of the Soviet past. Memory matters to everyone: both to those who refuse to let themselves or others forget the crimes of the past and the suffering of the victims, and to those who take pride in that past. It is not simply a matter of knowing something — Wiesel was right about that — achieving understanding is much more difficult. We can see how declared aims and ideological attitudes continue to change in our own time. From “Holocaust denial” — until quite recently, apologists for German nationalism claimed that Jews had not been exterminated and had themselves invented both the camps and the crematoria in order to slander innocent Germans (there were even claims that Jews themselves had organised the mass murder of Jews to spite the Aryans) — to contemporary proposals by Alternative for Germany not to teach about Hitlerism in schools and instead devote more attention to Bismarck. Germany’s far-right politicians are now closer to the cynical attitude: “Here’s your beer, here’s your ham, and what happened yesterday is in the past” (the ever-relevant words of a song by Yuliy Kim). No one is saying that it did not happen: it did. The only question is how to regard it, how to understand it. The militarist and nationalist Bismarck is, for the AfD, something good, something to take pride in, while schoolchildren need not be told about certain costs of twentieth-century history: enough already, so much has been said about it. The lavish funeral held in Belgrade with military honours for Ratko Mladić, convicted by the Hague Tribunal of crimes against humanity, is a striking manifestation of the contemporary conflict over memory: for some, the victims and witnesses of crimes matter; for others, what matters is the glorification of war criminals. Everyone wants to remember — but they remember different things and understand the past differently. Those who are erecting ever more monuments to Stalin in the Russian Federation obviously want to remind people of him, often making no attempt to conceal the fact that Stalinism was terror. They simply like terror and want to put it back on a pedestal. And they are prepared to remember the Gulag as well — not to deny its existence, but to explain it in their own way, interpreting it within the framework of the “inadmissibility of distorting the history of the USSR.” Thus, for example, one can hold an academic conference in a former Soviet camp, highlighting “examples of the extraordinary courage and patriotism of our compatriots, whose military and labour achievements have more than once become a central theme of academic conferences organised for ten years by the Perm-36 Museum-Reserve.” But telling the history of the Stalinist era as it was seen by those who survived despite the terror, those who neither forgot nor forgave, is treated as extremism. This is why Memorial was banned and the Gulag History Museum in Moscow was closed. It is not memory that is forbidden — it is understanding that is forbidden, precisely what Elie Wiesel and many others sought to achieve through their testimonies. The struggle to foster an understanding that terror and war crimes are unacceptable does not end even when a verdict has been handed down by the Hague (or Nuremberg) Tribunal. Constant efforts are required not only to prevent people from forgetting, but also to show history — including the most recent history — through the eyes of victims of violence, those who suffered, and surviving witnesses. To show their truth rather than the perpetrator’s version: the perpetrator who does not even conceal what he is doing — who may even take pride in it — but who always has an explanation of his own, most often that he was forced to “strike first,” to assert his right to dominance, and so on. The perpetrators themselves are also eager to preserve the memory of violence — in military monuments, bas-reliefs and installations. The voices of those who suffered can be heard in their memories, accounts and testimonies, which must be collected and published, as is being done today by the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group’s “Voices of War” project and in human rights reports , which bring together the tragic experiences of Ukrainian women and men who have suffered as a result of Russia’s military aggression. Stephania KULAEVA First published on the Radio Svoboda blog Facebook Twitter Вконтакте

https://montenegro.osce.org/news/mission.body: News News Item OSCE-supported court simulation strengthens Montenegro’s judicial response to violence against women and girls Issued on: 13 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Mission to Montenegro Fields of work: Rule of law , Gender-based violence Strengthening the capacity of judicial professionals to handle cases of violence against women and girls in a victim-centered manner is essential to preventing secondary victimization and ensuring fair trials. As the OSCE Mission to Montenegro marks 20 years of co-operation with national institutions this year, it continues to support joint efforts to strengthen the institutional responses to such violence. In this context, the Mission, in co-operation with the Supreme Court and the Centre for Training in Judiciary and State Prosecution Service, organized a court simulation training in Budva from 9 to 11 October for 15 judicial and prosecutorial advisors on handling cases of violence against women and girls. Now in its fourth consecutive year, the simulation aims to strengthen institutional responses to violence against women and girls. Building on previous simulations on femicide, rape, stalking and marital rape, this year’s exercise focused on the practical application of international and national legal standards through a mock trial involving a case of violence against women and girls. Participants examined the key stages of criminal proceedings, including the assessment of evidence, the preparation of an indictment, the main hearing and the delivery of a judgment. Opening the event, Ms. Ljiljana Perkušić, Democratization Programme Manager of the OSCE Mission, highlighted the relevance of this year’s exercise in translating legal standards into practice, particularly in light of recent amendments to the Criminal Procedure Code, which further strengthen the victim-centered approach. Ms. Gordana Nikolić, Head of the Specialized Training Department at the Centre for Training in Judiciary and State Prosecution Service, expressed her gratitude to the Mission and the Supreme Court for their continued co-operation in organizing the training. She noted that the exercise provided valuable learning opportunities and contributed to reducing the risk of secondary victimization, while strengthening the capacity of the judiciary to address cases involving women who have experienced domestic violence. Ms. Bojana Bandović, advisor to the Supreme Court, noted that the simulation served as a platform for exchanging experiences and good practices, while also raising awareness of the complexity and seriousness of cases involving violence against women and girls. She emphasized the importance of addressing these cases without prejudice or stereotypes, with full respect for the dignity of victims and the principles of a fair trial. https://dushanbe.osce.org/news/programme.body: News News Item Young women from Tajikistan and Afghanistan explore leadership, diplomacy and peace through OSCE course From 5 to 9 October 2026, the OSCE held the second edition of its Advanced Course on Diplomacy, Leadership and Peace for Young Women in Dushanbe, fostering collaboration among 20 young women from Tajikistan and Afghanistan to strengthen their leadership skills and prepare them to contribute to diplomacy and peacebuilding. Issued on: 13 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe Fields of work: Gender equality , Youth From 5 to 9 October 2026, the OSCE held the second edition of its Advanced Course on Diplomacy, Leadership and Peace for Young Women in Dushanbe, fostering collaboration among 20 young women from Tajikistan and Afghanistan to strengthen their leadership skills and prepare them to contribute to diplomacy and peacebuilding. The course aimed to equip participants with the knowledge, practical skills and professional networks needed to take an active role in promoting peace and security across the OSCE region and beyond. Through peer-to-peer learning, intergenerational dialogue and discussions with experienced guest speakers, participants explored a range of issues, including artificial intelligence and diplomacy, peacebuilding, human rights, career development and resilience. They also exchanged experiences and discussed the challenges and opportunities facing young women pursuing careers in these fields. Parvathy Ramaswami (centre), United Nations Resident Coordinator in Tajikistan, leads the “Coffee Talk” session on Diplomacy, Leadership, and the Next Generation as part of the OSCE’s Advanced Course on Diplomacy, Leadership and Peace for Young Women, Dushanbe, 5 October 2026. “Today, Tajik women are not merely participants in political processes, but active, thoughtful and responsible contributors to public life, embodying national values and a culture of peace, dialogue and constructive co-operation,” said Mavsuma Muini, Deputy Chairperson of the Majlisi Namoyandagon, the lower chamber of Tajikistan’s Parliament. “The OSCE School of Diplomacy, Leadership and Peacebuilding for Young Women is a valuable initiative that helps promote women’s participation in diplomacy and public and political life and raise the status of women in society,” Muini added. Fejzo Numanaj, Acting Deputy Head of Office and Officer-in-Charge of the OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe, encouraged participants to recognize their leadership potential: “You are not the leaders of tomorrow. You are already leaders today, in your universities, your workplaces, and your communities.” He added: “Together with the Parliament of Tajikistan, the Government, the United Nations and civil society, we remain committed to ensuring that young women’s voices shape dialogue, decisions and solutions.” Group photo marking the launch of the OSCE’s second Advanced Course on Diplomacy, Leadership and Peace for Young Women, featuring 20 young women from Tajikistan and Afghanistan alongside senior women leaders from the Government of Tajikistan and representatives of international organizations, Dushanbe, 5 October 2026. The course concluded with participants expanding their professional networks and reaffirming their commitment to contributing to peace and security. By investing in young women’s leadership and fostering dialogue across generations, the OSCE seeks to promote their meaningful participation in diplomacy and peacebuilding and enable them to contribute to addressing shared security challenges. https://rfom.osce.org/representative-fre.body: Press release OSCE RFoM organized the 26th Central Asia Media Conference in Bishkek, held bilateral meetings with Kyrgyz authorities Date: 13 October 2026 Place: BISHKEK Source: OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media BISHKEK, 13 October 2026 – The OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media, in co-operation with OSCE field operations in the region, organized the 26 th Central Asia Media Conference in Bishkek on 9 and 10 October gathering participants from Central Asia, Mongolia and the broader OSCE region. Interactive discussions focused on information integrity and trusted information landscapes in the region, safety of journalists, legislative and regulatory frameworks, journalism education, and professional standards. The conference was opened by the OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media, Ambassador Jan Braathu; Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Kyrgyz Republic Kairat Tursunkulov; Deputy Minister of Culture, Information, and Youth Policy of the Kyrgyz Republic Salkyn Sarnogoeva; and the Head of the OSCE Programme Office in Bishkek, Ambassador Volker Frobarth. “There are multiple challenges journalists face in their work throughout the OSCE region, including Central Asia. However, our responses to these challenges must remain firmly grounded in fundamental rights, including freedom of expression and media freedom. Open discussion about the importance of media freedom and its impact on our common security is crucial,” Ambassador Braathu said in his opening remarks. During his visit to Bishkek, Representative Braathu held bilateral meetings with the Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Kyrgyz Republic, Kairat Tursunkulov; the First Deputy Minister of Justice, Saira Yzakova; and the Chairman of the Service for Regulation and Supervision in the Communication Sector under the Ministry of Digital Development and Innovative Technologies, Altynbek Toktorbaev. On 10 and 11 October, the Office of the OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media partnered with the Bishkek Academy for the Academy’s annual alumni conference focussing on “Artificial Intelligence, Climate Change and Sustainable Development”. The RFoM Office’s work in the areas of media and AI was discussed at the conference within the Central Asian framework. The Office also laid out strategies to promote stronger climate and environmental journalism, and presented the RFoM/UNESCO joint publication “ Reporting the Environment: A Practical Manual for Journalists ”. Furthermore, the conference provided an opportunity to present the translation of OSCE Ministerial Council Decision No. 3/18 on the Safety of Journalists into five Central Asian languages and Mongolian, and discuss the implementation of the principles included in the Decision. “A commitment adopted at the international level needs to reach the people and institutions that are in a position to give it practical effect. And that means bringing the commitment not only geographically closer, but also linguistically closer, to those stakeholders. This is why translating MC Decision 3/18 into Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Tajik, Turkmen, Uzbek and Mongolian is part of the implementation process and a step towards national ownership,” concluded Braathu. The OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media observes media developments in all 57 OSCE participating States. He provides early warning on violations of freedom of expression and media freedom and promotes full compliance with OSCE media freedom commitments. https://odihr.osce.org/news/odihr/668634.body: News News Item ODIHR and OSCE PA launch guidelines to strengthen participation of people with disabilities in parliaments Issued on: 12 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights , OSCE Parliamentary Assembly Fields of work: Democratization , Tolerance and non-discrimination The OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) and the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly (OSCE PA) launched a new publication in Warsaw on 12 October 2026 to help parliaments identify and remove barriers to the full and effective participation of people with disabilities. People with disabilities remain underrepresented in national parliaments across the OSCE region and continue to face barriers to participation. Addressing these barriers means examining how people can contribute to parliamentary work, influence legislation and hold governments to account, alongside ensuring access to parliamentary buildings and information. “People with disabilities must be able to shape the laws and decisions that affect their lives. Parliaments need to examine their own rules and practices and work with people with disabilities to remove barriers to participation,” said Zaruhi Batoyan, Member of the National Assembly of the Republic of Armenia. Guidelines on Advancing disability-inclusive parliaments: an assessment methodology and insights from the OSCE region draws on a joint ODIHR/OSCE PA survey conducted in 2024. It combines survey findings and examples of good practice with a methodology covering representation, law-making, oversight and access, helping parliaments identify priorities and take practical steps towards reform. “Accessibility is part of everyday parliamentary work, from receiving information to taking part in debates and committee meetings. The test is whether people with disabilities can contribute on equal terms and have their voices reflected in decisions,” said Dastan Bekeshev, Member of the Jogorku Kenesh of the Kyrgyz Republic. Parliamentarians and civil society representatives shared experiences from the OSCE region and discussed how the methodology can be applied in practice. The publication was launched at a side event organized by ODIHR and the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly during the 2026 Warsaw Human Dimension Conference . https://hcnm.osce.org/news/hcnm/668601.body: News News Item OSCE High Commissioner on National Minorities visits Kosovo Issued on: 12 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE High Commissioner on National Minorities Fields of work: Conflict prevention and resolution , Human rights , National minority issues , Tolerance and non-discrimination , Gender equality OSCE High Commissioner on National Minorities Christophe Kamp visited Kosovo on 9 October 2026 to exchange with central and local authorities on recent developments that affected the situation of non-majority communities. In Prishtinë/Priština, Kamp met with Prime Minister Albin Kurti to continue their conversation on the importance of finding effective modalities to consult non-majority communities on policies and issues affecting them. The High Commissioner also met with the Mayor of North Mitrovica, Milan Radojević, to discuss recent developments in his municipality, particularly related to property rights and dialogue between central and local authorities. Kamp also held an exchange of views with the heads of KFOR, EULEX, the EU Office, and UNMIK. https://kloop.kg/blog/2026/10/13/politbl.body: Facebook Twitter VK Telegram WhatsApp МВД Кыргызстана сообщило о задержании Сыргака Кенжебаева, автора youtube-канала «Эр-Сыргак» — последнюю пару месяцев он критиковал власть и рассказывал, как сотрудничал с братом президента Садыра Жапарова Сабыром. По его словам Сабыр Джапаров вместе с сыном в своем «офисе» решал «политические вопросы» и влиял на таможню. МВД подозревает Кенжебаева в призывах к массовым беспорядкам и мошенничестве. Якобы Кенжебаев взял у некой М.Н. 150 тысяч долларов для совместной предпринимательской деятельности. Его объявили в розыск. Ведомство настаивает, что за границей Кенжебаев скрывался от уголовного преследования, и публиковал «провокационные материалы». По версии следствия, он призывал к массовым беспорядкам и последующему захвату власти. Не первое похищение за границей Задержание Кенжебаева, находившегося за границей, и последующий вывоз в Кыргызстан — не первая попытка лишить его свободы. И у его задержаний всегда кроме обвинения, которое в его адрес озвучивает следствие, есть и политическая подоплека. На данный период — его критика власти и объявление себя оппозицией Садыру Жапарову. Ранее Кенжебаев уже сообщал, что власти пытались задержать его в Камбодже 31 августа. Тогда он в одном из стримов сообщил, что на его задержание со своими подчиненными прибыл лично начальник главного управления уголовного розыска МВД Улан Айтбаев. Вместе с ним на пяти джипах приехали местная полиция, сотрудники спецслужб и консульства. Матраимов после задержания, 2024 год. А вот предыдущее задержание Кенжебаева было связано с противостоянием с экс-зампредом кыргызской таможни Райымбеком Матраимовым. Сыргак Кенжебаев — бизнесмен, создавший таможенный терминал «Юнилаб». Изначально проект выглядел многообещающим, но столкнулся с искусственно созданными проблемами, после которых новыми владельцами терминала стали люди из окружения экс-зампреда таможни Райымбека Матраимова . Бизнес-партнер Кенжебаева описал ту сделку как «рейдерский захват». Когда бывшая супруга Кенжебаева экс-депутатка Ширин Айтматова начала антикоррупционную кампанию против Райымбека Матраимова, Кенжебаева похитили из Алматы и оставили под арестом в Кыргызстане . Тогда следствие настаивало, что его задержали за якобы мошенничество. Заявление на него написал гражданин Китая, уверявший, что Кенжебаев завладел 350 000 долларов. По словам Айтматовой, это был некий Муталиф, китайский бизнесмен уйгурского происхождения. Она подозревала, что он из корпорации АКА, с ним Кенжебаева познакомил депутат Алиарбек Абжалиев, сват тогдашнего президента Сооронбая Жээнбекова. У президента Жапарова хорошие отношения с Абдукадыром. Вот они вместе на церемонии начала строительства дорогущей мечети в пригороде Бишкека. Корпорация «АКА» принадлежит Хабибулле Абдукадыру — влиятельному китайскому бизнесмену и герою журналистского расследования о контрабанде. Он сват Райымбека Матраимова и так или иначе взаимодействовал с тремя последними кыргызскими президентами — Алмазбеком Атамбаевым, Сооронбаем Жээнбековым и Садыром Жапаровым. Ради безопасности Кенжебаева Айтматова прекратила публичную деятельность. Кенжебаев смог выйти на свободу только после протестов в октябре 2020 года, когда протестующие освободили Садыра Жапарова. Однако в том же месяце всех освобожденных вернули в колонию — кроме Садыра Жапарова. Спустя какое-то время Кенжебаева все же освободили и он, по его словам, пытался сотрудничать с властью по привлечению в Кыргызстан инвестиций — факт коммуникации с Кенжебаевым подтвердил Садыр Жапаров. В начале августа Кенжебаев открыл канал на YouTube и начал публиковать видеоролики о происходящем в Кыргызстане. В одном из них он рассказал, что Сабыр Джапаров и Рустам Жапаров, брат и сын президента, а также другие его близкие родственники, якобы «решают политические вопросы Кыргызстана» и контролируют таможню из так называемого «офиса». При этом Сабыр Джапаров и другие близкие родственники президента никогда официально не занимали никакие госдолжности. Брат президента «Сабыр Джапаров там уселся и организовал офис. И не только он. Братья и члены семьи Жапаровых обосновались там. Вызывают к себе любого чиновника, увольняют любого чиновника, и именно там решают многие политические вопросы Кыргызстана [...] Сын Сабыра, Азат Джапаров, с отцом и другими своими братьями, кормятся из одной кормушки. Они наживаются, оставляя народ ни с чем и продавая золото в чистом виде за границу», — утверждает Кенжебаев. В свою очередь, президент Садыр Жапаров в своем интервью журналисту Али Токтакунову, ушел от прямого ответа на вопрос о том, контролирует ли его брат, Сабыр Джапаров, таможню Кыргызстана. Вместо этого он перешел на личность Кенжебаева, негативно высказавшись в его адрес, а поле этого завери л, что «Жапаровы не путали свой карман с государственным». https://kloop.kg/blog/2026/10/13/po-puti.body: Facebook Twitter VK Telegram WhatsApp Когда полгода назад налоговая выпустила расследование о клане Ташиевых и схемах на «Кыргызнефтегазе», невольно появлялся вопрос — не будут ли авторов расследования преследовать также, как и авторов другого расследования на ту же тему? Еще в 2022 году, 20 января, издание «Temirov Live» рассказало о «схеме Ташиевых» , которая позволила заработать компании, связанной с главой ГКНБ Камчыбеком Ташиевым, 37 млн сомов всего за два дня. 22 января журналист-расследователь Болот Темиров был задержан , а правоохранители подкинули ему наркотики, которые потом сами же и нашли. В тот же день Камчыбек Ташиев обвинил журналистов расследователей во лжи. 23 января Ташиев даже дал пресс-конференцию, где на доске подробно объяснил, как работает предприятие по продаже мазута. Само расследование стало предтечей масштабного давления на всю команду журналистов, насильного изгнания Темирова из страны и массовых арестов сотрудников. Но расследование налоговой, опубликованное после освобождения Камчыбека Ташиева с его должностей, привело к допросам и арестам фигурантов дела. Однако, полгода спустя публикации лицо и автор расследования Анарбек Катаганов рассказал — его тоже преследовали за расследование о Ташиевых. Более того, его даже задерживали — однако задержание официально связано с пострадавшим во время штурма резиденции бывшего президента Алмазбека Атамбаева милиционером Саматом Курманкуловым. « Вся эта история — спланированная провокация из-за моего расследования про «Кыргызнефтегаз» и семью Ташиевых. С момента выхода видео мне поступали угрозы, а затем меня попытались сломать через грязную подставу со старым делом 2015 года и 1,5-минутным звонком генералу Самату Курманкулову, которого использовали вслепую. Силовики сработали по ложному доносу мгновенно », — рассказал Катаганов в своих соцсетях. Подробнее он рассказал в приложенном к посту интервью. Если опустить детали, получается что Катаганова задержали за звонок Курманкулову, а после выхода из СИЗО источник сообщил ему, что все это связано с Ташиевыми. Катаганов объясняет — ему после выхода видео налоговой угрожали, говорили «зачем ты снял про Ташиева, он наш брат». По его словам, в Жалал-Абаде его «вообще убить хотели». А вот задержанного по делу о «Кыргызнефтегазе» брата Камчыбека Ташиева Шайырбека Ташиева, отпустили под домарест в июле. Источники до того сообщали СМИ, что Шайырбек Ташиев ни дня не провел в СИЗО-1, куда был определен судом. Вместо этого он был в ИВС ГУВД Бишкека. Еще в апреле МВД сообщало, что задержанный сегодня по делу «Кыргызнефтегаза» экс-депутат Шайырбек Ташиев должен возместить государству за нанесенный ущерб 4,1 млрд сомов. Это порядка 46 млн долларов. И президент комментировал это дело — Садыр Жапаров сказал , что Шайырбек Ташиев «должен все вернуть», и только потом выйдет на свободу. Только вот в сентябре от адвоката Ташиева Жыргалбека Бабаева стало известно , что сумму ущерба пересмотрят. МВД сообщило, что Шайырбек Ташиев возместил «основную часть ущерба» — однако сумму не назвали. https://adcmemorial.org/en/news/khpg-new.body: Facebook Twitter Вконтакте A roundup of news from the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group (KHPG), one of the oldest human rights organizations in Ukraine. Since 2014, KHPG has been documenting war crimes in eastern Ukraine, and since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, it has been documenting events that show signs of crimes under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes) across all regions of Ukraine. KHPG is one of the founders of the T4P (Tribunal for Putin) initiative, which brings together more than two dozen organizations with the aim of holding Russia accountable for the crimes committed. Russian Education as a Tool for Militarization In occupied Crimea, discussions are underway about the operation of cadet and “Cossack” classes for schoolchildren, the expansion of the “Little Cadets and Cossacks” project for preschoolers, the role of military training camps, and cooperation between Crimean schools and the Russian occupation security agencies. Thirteen kindergartens, with groups of children aged five to seven, are participating in the propaganda project “Little Cadets and Cossacks.” In the temporarily occupied territories of Donetsk Oblast, Russian paratroopers have organized an event where they demonstrated military equipment to minors. In occupied Skadovsk, cadets at School No. 1 were provided with uniforms for classes operating under the patronage of Rosgvardiya (the Russian National Guard). In effect, schoolchildren will be wearing uniforms resembling those of Russian security forces. “The problem is not only that military culture is being imposed on children. The use of uniforms closely resembling those worn by Russian security forces creates a dangerous situation under conditions of occupation and hostilities: it becomes significantly more difficult to distinguish civilian children from members of Russian security forces,” the Ukrainian National Resistance Center notes. In an overview article, KHPG examines the ongoing militarization and indoctrination of Ukrainian children by the occupying power. Read in Ukrainian: Російська освіта як плацдарм для мілітаризації A Family Affair: Russia Persecutes Entire Families in Occupied Territories Russian authorities widely employ the practice of detaining entire families in occupied territories. This makes it easier for Russian security services to exert pressure on those who oppose the regime. When charges are based on self-incriminating statements, detainees can be forced to sign virtually any testimony if their mother, son, or daughter is being held in a neighboring cell. KHPG recounts the persecution of seven families: Valentyn Maliar and his sister Tetiana Behei (Maliar), together with their children Anatolii Rossikhin and Olha Behei; married couple Serhii Kozlov and Yevheniia Samoilova; Viktoriia Strilets and her daughter Oleksandra Strilets; Oleksii Demianenko and his daughter Anzhelika Demianenko; Anna Murdidi, her son Artem Murdidi and his wife Anna Voshkoder; married couple Oleh Platonov and Nataliia Poliukh; and Volodymyr Perzhynskyi and his son Mark Perzhynskyi. Read in Ukrainian: Справи сімейні: росіяни переслідують на окупованих територіях цілі родини Detention Extended for Women Charged in the “First Female Hizb ut-Tahrir Case” Four Crimean Tatar women arrested a year ago, on October 15, 2025—Esma Nimetullaeva, Nasibe Saidova, Elviza Alieva, and Fevzie Osmanova—have had their pre-trial detention extended. It was previously reported that FSB officers had completed the “preliminary investigation” into the case of the Crimean detainees. According to sources, in addition to Article 205.5 of the Russian Criminal Code (concerning involvement in the activities of Hizb ut-Tahrir), the Crimean Tatar women are charged with preparing to seize power by force under Article 278 of the Russian Criminal Code. Esma Nimetullaeva , who lived in Bakhchysarai, worked as a pastry chef and was raising five underage daughters. Her husband, Crimea Solidarity activist Remzi Nimetullaev, was first detained in November 2021 in Sevastopol, when he came to meet a lawyer outside a detention center following the lawyer’s release from administrative detention. Remzi Nimetullaev was detained for a second time in August 2023, following a wave of mass searches. This time, he and five other Crimea Solidarity activists were accused of organizing the activities of Hizb ut-Tahrir. Elviza Alieva worked as a cashier at a bakery in Simferopol. She was also a fourth-year Management student at the so-called Crimean Federal University. Nasibe Saidova , the daughter of a well-known imam in Crimea, was in her final year of college, studying education, and worked with a nursery group at a kindergarten. Fevzie Osmanova worked in the family business, a shop. According to the Crimean Tatar Resource Center, as of March 2026, at least 52 women were known to have been subjected to political persecution by the Russian authorities and were being held in pre-trial detention centers or penal colonies. More details are available in the KHPG article. Read in English: Russia’s ‘trial’ begins of Crimean Tatar mother of five and three young women for ‘trying to violently seize power’ Analytical report within the framework of the KHPG project ‘Strengthening Public Oversight and Accountability of State Institutions in Ukraine’, 2025–2026 KHPG has published three sections of a comprehensive study on the human rights situation in Ukraine in 2025–2026, covering trends under wartime conditions, challenges in combating corruption, and the protection of the rights of vulnerable groups. The study traces developments in human rights protection in Ukraine from the beginning of the Russian-Ukrainian war in 2014, examines changes following the full-scale invasion in February 2022, and identifies trends in 2025–2026. Key issues addressed in the report: The report examines the narrowing of the space for civil and political freedoms under the pretext of martial law, the absence of systematic dialogue between the authorities and civil society, pressure on the opposition and attempts to subordinate the judiciary. It analyses the unconstitutional application of National Security and Defence Council (NSDC) sanctions against Ukrainian citizens and cases of unlawful deprivation of citizenship without transparent procedures or judicial oversight. In the sphere of freedom of speech, the report records the growing state monopolisation of the information space through the retention of the ‘United News Telethon’, the removal of patriotic opposition TV channels ( Espreso, Priamyi, Channel 5 ) from digital broadcasting, and pressure by law enforcement and security agencies (the SBU and the SBI) on investigative journalists and bloggers (the cases of Bihus.Info, Yu. Butusov, B. Bereza and Slidstvo.Info ). At the same time, it emphasises that society has retained its capacity for peaceful resistance (the ‘cardboard protests’ of 2025–2026). The third section of the report, “Human Rights in Ukraine 2025 and the First Half of 2026. Rights of Vulnerable Groups”, analyzes the situation of vulnerable groups in Ukraine during the war in 2025–2026, including sex workers, people who use drugs, women living with HIV, and LGBTIQ+ people. It highlights systemic discrimination, barriers to healthcare, legal challenges and recommendations. Monitoring networks continue to document hate speech, discrimination, harassment, and intolerance-motivated offences against LGBTIQ+ people based on sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, and sex characteristics (SOGIESC). At the same time, significant progress has been made in recognizing the situation and needs of LGBTIQ+ people as a social group in legislation and public policy. The number of legal and regulatory acts explicitly prohibiting discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and/or gender identity has been steadily increasing.

https://www.rferl.org/a/germany-trial-no.body: Ukraine Germany To Start Nord Stream 'War Crime' Trial With Prosecutors Blaming Ukrainian 'State Authorities' By Ray Furlong and RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service October 13, 2026 09:09 CET Germany To Start Nord Stream 'War Crime' Trial With Prosecutors Blaming Ukrainian 'State Authorities' Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Policemen escort Serhii K. to a hearing with a prosecutor in Karlsruhe, Germany, on November 28, 2025. After four years of speculation, leaks, and briefings by anonymous sources, the world is finally about to hear evidence given publicly under oath in a German courtroom about how the Nord Stream gas pipelines were blown up -- in a case that could prove politically explosive. German prosecutors have identified seven Ukrainian suspects, but just one of them is in the dock in the trial beginning on October 14. He is named as Serhii K. in court documents that say he is suspected of a being an accomplice to a war crime. That classification has caused outrage. But German prosecutors have further raised the stakes by stating the suspects were operating "on behalf of state authorities in Ukraine." SEE ALSO: Ukrainian Arrested In Connection To 2022 Nord Stream Explosions Kyiv has always strictly denied any involvement in the attack, which damaged crucial energy infrastructure serving Germany -- one of its most important military backers in its fight since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Serhii K., who has been identified elsewhere as Serhiy Kuznetsov, says he is innocent. 'Two Crazy Military Men' Nord Stream is majority-owned by Russia's state-controlled Gazprom and co-financed by major European energy companies. It was constructed to deliver Russian gas directly to Germany, bypassing transit states such as Ukraine and Poland, which had tense relations with Moscow. The suspected sabotage and subsequent gas leaks happened in September 2022, rendering the pipelines as inoperable. Western governments originally accused Russia of carrying out the blasts, but German investigators started forming a case that said a group of Ukrainian divers hired a yacht and planted explosives on the seabed. They say Kuznetsov, a former military officer, was the ringleader. "At the end of February 2022, he and other military personnel, on behalf of state authorities in Ukraine, developed the plan," says a summary of the indictment released by prosecutors. "The aim was to permanently halt gas deliveries via the pipelines and prevent Russia from using the revenue from the natural gas trade to finance its war efforts." The prosecutors have not stated publicly the full extent of the alleged conspiracy. The full indictment contains some further details, according to three German media outlets that say they have seen it: public-service TV station ARD and two print-era heavyweights, Sueddeutsche Zeitung and Die Zeit. SEE ALSO: Ukraine Grants Bail To Military Officer Who Reportedly 'Coordinated' Nord Stream Sabotage They all reported that, while in custody in Italy, Kuznetsov had phoned his wife in Kyiv and investigators were secretly listening in as he said he'd been advised by a lawyer that it was time to admit this had been "an official military operation." His commander should state that they were not just "two crazy military men." Kuznetsov's Italian lawyer, Nicola Canestrini, has played down the importance of this evidence, saying there was "no smoking gun" in the case. "It is hard to believe that, after Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine, a German court should hold a war crimes trial against a Ukrainian serviceman," he added in comments to RFE/RL. The three German media outlets named Roman Chervinskiy as Serhii K.'s commander, and his name also appeared in multiple earlier media reports citing intelligence sources. Chervinskiy told RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service in July that "the Germans actually have no evidence whatsoever that Serhii took part in this operation, if it even took place." Another suspect, identified by Germany as Vladimir Z. , is currently in custody in Croatia, where he is fighting extradition. He was previously detained in Poland but was freed when a Polish judge ruled that if Ukraine were responsible for the Nord Stream attack, it was a "just" act. A professional diver identified by his Polish lawyers as Volodymyr Zhuravlyov, he was working in Croatia as an adviser on a Hollywood movie about Nord Stream. During the trial, the prosecution will have to lay out its evidence for a conspiracy and the full extent of it. "That is the crucial question: How much came from the top of the Ukrainian political system or how much was prepared by some insiders in the intelligence service?" Stefan Meister, a specialist on Russia and Eastern Europe at the German Council on Foreign Relations, told RFE/RL. SEE ALSO: Exclusive: A Russian Blueprint For A Cold, Dark Winter In Ukraine "The key political question is the role of Zelenskyy and the presidential administration. And there we still have no proof that they were really involved," he added. Kuznetsov's German lawyer, Jes Meyer-Lohkamp, said prosecutors "have not provided any direct, conclusive evidence of our client's involvement" and that the German court will have to determine whether Nord Stream was actually a legitimate military target. The Hanseatic Higher Regional Court in Hamburg has scheduled two hearings every week until at least February, with no specified end date yet. German Support For Ukraine As the case unfolds, it will also feed into bitter disputes in Germany about ongoing support for Ukraine. The main opposition party, Alternative for Germany (AfD), is highly critical of this support and calls for close ties to Russia instead. Evidence of Ukrainian involvement in the Nord Stream attack "would strengthen the AfD's argumentation against this support for Ukraine," said Meister. "They have all these narratives about Ukrainian corruption, a failed state.... It would resonate also in parts of German society." The AfD has recently won key regional elections and is piling the pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government over Ukraine, immigration, and economic concerns. Merz's response has been to double-down on his current policies, including on Ukraine. Most recently, he was in Kyiv on October 4 with a new aid package including joint production of interceptors to shoot down Russian jet-powered drones. Mikhaylo Honchar, head of the Kyiv-based Strategy XXI Global Studies Center, told RFE/RL this would likely continue regardless of what comes out at the trial. "If you take into consideration real Russian policy, which is directed against the EU and NATO, and Russia's anti-German rhetoric, I think the government of Germany will avoid steps which would undermine the bilateral relationship" with Ukraine, he said. He added that the prosecution case was "absurd," citing German media reports that the attack may have been a Russian false-flag operation. But in any case, Honchar said, a guilty verdict would be met with a clear response in Ukraine. "Many people will say: 'If our guys did it, they are heroes.'" The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:11:49 0:00 Direct link 128 kbps | MP3 64 kbps | MP3 Pop-out player The Briefing: The EU’s October Summit -- Sanctions, Enlargement, And Financing Ukraine As European Union leaders gather in Brussels on October 15-16, the main media focus will most likely be on the almighty EU budget battle as the 27 prime ministers and presidents make their first real stab at finding a consensus for the next long-term EU budget for 2028-2034. They will fail, as summits are already planned for November and December to potentially seal the deal. But there is no guarantee that they will strike an agreement then either, as the draft proposal of 1.6 trillion euros ($1.78 trillion) is dividing northern “frugals,” who want more cuts, and the rest, who want the budget to increase or at least stay the same. The fight over cash in Brussels tends to be the fiercest and most drawn-out, and will divert much of the EU’s attention away from the bigger international issues confronting the bloc, such as the war in Ukraine and even its own process of admitting new members. Yet, the draft EU summit conclusions, seen by RFE/RL, still offer some hints about what the bloc hopes to do on a number of foreign policy issues in the coming months. Financing Ukraine There was a sudden political storm brewing in both Brussels and Kyiv when Ukrainian officials began warning in early September of a military funding shortfall of as much as $27 billion. Much confusion ensued as various other numbers were cited, and Ukrainian and European officials started studying what the issue was and whether the 90 billion euros ($100 billion) that the EU had agreed to lend Kyiv earlier in the year for 2026 and 2027 -- with 45 billion euros earmarked for each year -- would need to be restructured, notably by bringing forward some of the money allocated for 2027. EU sources familiar with the discussions told RFE/RL that the changing estimates of Ukraine’s needs reflect the rapidly evolving situation. They explained that the cost of the military equipment Ukraine intends to purchase is rising, as are expenditures on military personnel salaries and compensation payments for the families of fallen soldiers. However, through national budget reallocations and financial support from other international partners, Kyiv has been finding ways to cover its most urgent needs. This was also confirmed in the draft EU conclusions, which note that the European Council “welcomes the ongoing disbursements to Ukraine from the EUR 90 billion Ukraine Support Loan for 2026 and 2027, including the recent disbursements of EUR 5.34 billion. It welcomes the fact that the means to cover Ukraine’s budget and defense needs for 2026 have been identified.” But this is not the end of the story. While 2026 is covered for now, EU diplomats believe that Ukraine will use up the remaining 45 billion euros in the first half of 2027, meaning that the gap avoided this winter will likely reappear a year later. That means the EU will have to find more money, as the bloc’s next long-term budget, which is expected to include more funding for Ukraine, won’t kick in until 2028. It is therefore very possible that the discussion about using the billions in frozen Russian assets held in the bloc will come into play again at some point. This definitely won’t happen at this week’s summit, but the issue could return to the agenda at the summits scheduled for November and December and is almost certain to resurface early next year. Symbolic Sanctioning And Estonian Embarrassment The draft summit conclusions mention that “the European Union remains determined to further increase pressure on Russia so that it stops its brutal war of aggression and engages in meaningful negotiations towards peace. The European Council welcomes the recent adoption of the 21st sanctions package and of a substantial number of further listings of individuals and entities.” Despite what initially looks like a straightforward call for more sanctions on Moscow, there is a subtle but important difference here. In previous years, and at earlier summits, EU leaders have consistently pushed for further measures, meaning additional sanctions packages. But after the difficulties that dogged the 21st round of sanctions , which were only approved after a lot of wrangling in July, it is clear that the bloc is inching away from adopting new economic sanctions and is instead now essentially just adding more names to its blacklist. And while the headline figure of almost 1,600 new listings, officially approved on October 12, sounds impressive -- marking the largest-ever addition to the EU sanctions list -- those targeted are hardly household names. In fact, they all belong to Russia's domestic military-industrial complex, which has hardly any assets in the bloc to begin with. But not everything has been plain sailing, even with these seemingly straightforward listings. Embarrassingly, Estonia, a sanctions hawk, asked for one company and one person to be removed from the originally proposed list seen by RFE/RL. The entity was the Solikamsk plant, which exports rare earth materials and the individual was its CEO, Ruslan Dimukhamedov. With most of the company’s EU exports going to Estonia, the Baltic state confirmed that it had pushed the bloc not to sanction it. In a statement given to RFE/RL, the Estonian EU representation noted that “the company provides NPM Silmet, which is based in Estonia, with strategically important materials for Europe. European industries who are reliant on NPM Silmet include electric vehicle manufacturers, wind turbine producers, and the electronics, automotive, and aviation sectors across the European Union.” The statement also noted that “NPM Silmet is actively looking for alternative sources for the materials it imports from Russia. Estonia will revisit listing the Russian company and person next year.” The whole affair illustrates how even the most ardent supporters of Ukraine in the EU have national economic interests tied to Russia that they simply won’t compromise on, making a mockery of the bloc's push for tougher sanctions on the Kremlin. Visas For Russians While traditional sanctions policy appears to be taking a backseat for now, the issue of restricting more Russians from entering the EU is gaining traction in Brussels. The EU is still working on banning Russians who have fought in Ukraine from entering the bloc on Schengen tourist visas, with the draft summit conclusions calling for “the swift implementation of the measures concerning Russian ex-combatants.” This is the most obvious sign that even Mediterranean countries like France, Italy, and Spain, which rely heavily on tourism, are moving closer to agreeing to measures that could require Russian applicants to submit military service documents when applying for Schengen tourist visas in the future. https://www.rferl.org/a/trump-russia-die.body: News Zelenskyy Accuses Russia Of Breaking Trump's Cease-Fire On Energy Strikes By Alex Raufoglu October 13, 2026 02:09 CET Updated October 13, 2026 12:58 CET Zelenskyy Accuses Russia Of Breaking Trump's Cease-Fire On Energy Strikes Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Russia pounded Ukraine with air strikes overnight on October 12-13, killing at least three people in the city of Kharkiv. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia of failing to adhere to President Donald Trump's cease-fire on air strikes targeting energy infrastructure as officials across Europe looked for clarity on the truce and the US leader's deal with Moscow to allow Russian diesel exports. Trump has maintained that the truce -- which he unilaterally announced on October 11 -- is in place despite a lack of confirmation from either side. Zelenskyy, who was quoted as saying the truce was "news to me," said in a social media post that, over the past two days, Ukraine has held back from striking Russian oil refineries as demanded by Trump. But, he added, Russia has not acted in kind. "During this time, the Russians have attacked both our energy facilities and our critical infrastructure, sending absolutely clear signals ⁠that they have no intention of refraining from strikes on Ukraine," Zelenskyy wrote on October 13. Later on October 12, Zelenskyy said Ukraine is willing to halt attacks on Russian refining operations if Moscow agrees to stop its strikes on Ukrainian energy systems. Speaking to reporters on the White House lawn on October 12, Trump told reporters: “They agreed [to the cease-fire]. You know why? Because I said, ‘You agree’ -- that's why. They agreed because I said they agreed, and that thing has to get settled.” SEE ALSO: House Republicans Move To Block Trump's Russia Diesel Deal Asked by RFE/RL about reports of Russian violations of the agreement, Trump said he was “not sure about that,” adding that Zelenskyy and Putin “have to get together and end that ridiculous war.” Kyiv Power Plant Hit Just hours after Trump's announcement, Russian drones hit a power plant in Kyiv and energy facilities in the city of Kharkiv, sowing further confusion on the situation. That prompted Zelenskyy to tell a security conference in Warsaw that "if Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then Russia must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure and stop killing our people." Russian air strikes continued on October 13, with Ukrainian authorities saying at least three people were killed and 11 others injured when a Russian missile hit a four-story residential building. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the capital also came under attack. It was not clear if Russia targeted any energy facilities in its attacks. Trump also defended an agreement on allowing diesel exports from Russia, which he first announced after a conversation with Putin on October 9. He argued that Europe had continued buying Russian energy despite the war. While some European countries do still purchase Russian natural gas and crude oil, imports have fallen dramatically as the continent weans itself off Russian supplies. Trump has said that under the deal, the United States would immediately import 300,000 metric tons of Russian diesel, with millions more expected to follow. As part of the move, the US Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control issued a General License 135, authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel, including imports into the United States, through April 7, 2027. "The rest of the world should be on the side of the victim and certainly those countries who want to still be strong for the concept of freedom," she said. Ahead of November 3 midterm elections, the Trump administration has presented the deal as a response to high fuel costs. But the move has sparked a wave of criticism from Democrats and even some Republican officials, who warned it would embolden Putin to continue his war on Ukraine. Trump dismissed the Republicans who criticized the deal as lawmakers who "can't really be serious.” SEE ALSO: Exclusive: A Russian Blueprint For A Cold, Dark Winter In Ukraine Senators Push Back A bipartisan group of seven senators has urged the administration to reverse its decision, warning that Russian energy revenue helps finance Moscow's war against Ukraine. The US “should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians,” they said. The statement was signed by Republican Senators Susan Collins, Thom Tillis, John Curtis, and Lisa Murkowski, along with Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal, and Ron Wyden. On October 12, another Republican Senator Jerry Moran of Kansas warned that allowing Russian diesel imports risked “erasing our leverage, damaging our credibility with allies, and emboldening our adversaries.” Republican House Majority Whip Tom Emmer defended the president, calling the deal “another example of our president thinking out of the box” and describing it as another step toward resolving the war. Energy analysts who spoke with RFE/RL questioned whether the additional supplies could significantly affect prices before the vote. Mark Temnycky, a nonresident fellow at the Atlantic Council's Eurasia Center, told RFE/RL that the announced 300,000 metric tons of diesel would amount to roughly half a day's US consumption, based on figures from the US Energy Information Administration. SEE ALSO: Former US Diplomat Fried Warns Mixed Signals Could Undercut Russia Sanctions Temnycky questioned whether Russia could deliver the promised volumes, citing restrictions on production and exports following Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries. He warned that easing sanctions without securing concessions from Moscow could weaken international pressure on Russia and provide Moscow with potential revenue and a political victory for Putin. Ariel Cohen, managing director of energy, growth, and security at the International Tax and Investment Center, said Trump should use US leverage to secure a cease-fire rather than treat an energy agreement as a substitute for progress toward peace. Cohen added that any energy truce should be reciprocal, covering Ukrainian power-generation facilities and electricity grids as well as Russian energy ports, pipelines, and refineries. “It's either all energy infrastructure, including all the power generation and grid in Ukraine, versus in exchange for energy ports, energy pipelines, energy refineries in Russia,” he said. William Taylor, a former US ambassador to Ukraine who served under President George W. Bush and during Trump's first administration, told RFE/RL that a cease-fire could not take effect without agreement from both sides. https://cpj.org/2026/10/turkey-4-more-jo.body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email Istanbul, October 12, 2026—Turkey’s ongoing crackdown on independent media is continuing at an alarming pace with four more journalists arrested and placed under house arrest over the weekend on suspicion of publicly spreading disinformation , the Committee to Protect Journalists said Monday. On October 9, Turkish police questioned Mustafa Balcı and İsmail Saymaz from the independent Sözcü media outlet, freelancer Şaban Sevinç, and Murat Ağırel, who works for the independent Cumhuriyet and Onlar news outlets, about their reporting on a recent investment fund scandal . Mustafa Balcı (left) (Screenshot: Sözcü Televisyonu/YouTube) and Şaban Sevinç (Screenshot: Şaban Sevinç/YouTube) Later that same day, an Istanbul court arrested Balcı and Sevinç on suspicion of “publicly spreading disinformation.” Saymaz and Ağırel, who were released after questioning on October 9 under judicial control – meaning a foreign travel ban and regular check-ins with the police – were placed under house arrest on October 10 after the prosecution lodged an objection to their releases. “By arresting Mustafa Balcı and Şaban Sevinç and placing İsmail Saymaz and Murat Ağırel under house arrest on suspicion of publicly spreading disinformation, Turkey continues to erode press freedom at an alarming rate. We are reaching a crisis point with at least 22 journalists arrested or detained under the disinformation law this year alone,” said Özgür Öğret, CPJ’s Turkey representative. “All of the journalists who were either imprisoned or placed under house arrest must be immediately freed and Turkey’s disinformation law should be abolished without delay.” At the time of publishing, CPJ could not determine what content produced by Balcı and Sevinç formed the basis of their arrests. After he was summoned by the police to testify, Balcı said in a post on X that he believed he was going to be questioned about his reporting on the investment fund scandal. İsmail Saymaz (left) and Murat Ağırel (Screenshot: Sözcü Televizyonu/YouTube) Saymaz and Ağırel were questioned about their participation in a live broadcast on Sözcü TV on October 7. Writing in their regular columns in Sözcü and Cumhuriyet on Monday, they denied spreading disinformation. These new arrests come after Faruk Acar, deputy chair of the ruling AKP party in charge of publicity and media, threatened journalists who report so-called false news in comments posted on X on October 8. Turkish authorities have also blocked access to thousands of social media accounts belonging to journalists and rights defenders as part of the media crackdown. CPJ emailed the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office for comment but did not receive a reply. https://cpj.org/2026/10/at-least-37-jour.body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email New Delhi, October 12, 2026 — More than three dozen journalists were temporarily detained, and in some cases assaulted , while they were covering protests against the country’s chief election commissioner over allegations of voter-list manipulation in New Delhi, Ahmedabad, and Pune on October 10 and 11. In New Delhi, where the main protests broke out, at least 35 journalists were detained over the course of the next two days, according to CPJ’s review of news reports, direct interviews, and verified social media posts by editors, journalists, and their newsrooms. Two more journalists were detained while covering solidarity protests in other cities on October 10, including Alt News correspondent Kinjal in Ahmedabad and Scroll’s Divya Aslesha in Pune. Police continued detaining journalists even after Supreme Court justices won assurances from Solicitor-General Tushar Mehta on October 11 that lawyers, journalists, and other professionals would not be impeded in their professional duties. The court, which is due to hear the matter again on October 13, also directed that no one be detained except by procedure established by law. “CPJ’s research shows that, on October 10 and 11, Indian police detained at least 37 journalists while they were covering protests against the chief election commissioner — with several also being assaulted, heckled, or obstructed in their work,” said Kunal Majumder, CPJ’s Asia-Pacific program coordinator. “These incidents are deeply troubling and a blot on India’s democratic traditions. They violate international standards on press freedom and journalists’ constitutional rights, and also contradict the government’s assurance to the Supreme Court that journalists would not be impeded in their work. As the world’s largest democracy, India has a special responsibility to uphold press freedom, protect journalists from interference, and hold police officers accountable for assaulting or obstructing them.” The protests were called by the Cockroach Janta Party, a youth-led political movement, together with student groups and opposition parties, to demand the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar. Protesters allege that a nationwide revision of voter rolls has wrongly removed eligible voters, allegations that the Election Commission and the government deny. Delhi Police denied permission for the demonstration, citing inadequate notice and law-and-order concerns, and a prohibitory order barred gatherings in central New Delhi. Police also restricted access to dozens of metro stations, canceled some train services, and suspended internet services within about four kilometers (two and a half miles) of the Janpath–Kartavya Path area and around makeshift detention centers. Days before the protest, Delhi Police had issued guidelines for journalists asking them to display press cards prominently. Indian authorities deployed about 23,000 paramilitary personnel for the protests, including forces withdrawn from Jammu and Kashmir, West Bengal, and Chhattisgarh, along with at least 15,000 Delhi Police officers. In addition to detaining journalists, police dragged some reporters by their clothes and shoved others into buses , despite their display of press cards. Authorities also seized at least five phones, pressured at least one journalist to delete footage, and drove some to holding sites up to 65 kilometers (40 miles) away. At least five journalists were struck by police, according to their own accounts or their outlets’. On October 10, prominent Indian journalist Rana Ayyub posted on X that police threatened to detain her when she asked whether they were facilitating a man who was shouting abuse at protesters in their presence. Ayyub, a columnist for The Washington Post, told CPJ that, despite knowing she was a journalist, police beat her with a lathi (baton), resulting in injuries that are still causing her pain. The following journalists were detained over the two days, most while displaying press cards: On October 10, Delhi Police temporarily detained Scroll’s Ayush Tiwari and Shoaib Daniyal ; Business Standard’s Anushka Bhardwaj ; Newslaundry reporters Ashwine Kumar Singh, Astha Savyasachi, and Anmol Pritam and intern Anshu; Reuters’ Saurabh Sharma ; Navbharat Times’ Hritik Joshi and Rahul Charas ; BOOM’s Jagriti Trisha ; Shivang Shukla of Mo , India Today’s digital video platform; Molitics’ Neeraj Jha ; The Quint’s Sarthak Jaiswal ; Reporter TV’s Roshni Rajan and Farza TM ; independent journalists Shrishti Khanna and Prashant Pundir ; No Noise Stories’ Vivek Gupta ; and Alt News intern Agniva Ray . On October 11, police detained Indian Express Hindi reporters Shashwat, Siya, and Vijay ; Hindustan’s Ashish Singh ; Nayab World’s Nitin Katiyar ; Ulta Chasma founder Pragya Mishra ; and independent journalists Nidhi Suresh and M. Rajshekhar . Several journalists also were detained while covering protests at Connaught Place that day . Despite wearing press cards, Peek TV journalists Vedanta Agarwal and Sara Khan were filming police detaining protesters when officers dragged them away and detained them. Khan said that a male police officer grabbed her by the neck and pushed her toward a female officer. Police detained independent journalist Shyam Meera Singh after he was heckled and abused by Hindu rightwing activists. Shortly afterward, Singh’s X account, where he had been posting short videos of the protests, was withheld in India “in response to a legal demand,” according to the platform’s notice. The account remains visible outside India. Police also detained at least three journalists from Malayalam-language news channels on October 11 and released them hours later. Asianet News reporter Sajin A was detained and released after about half an hour, the outlet’s Delhi head, Prashanth Raghuvamsam, confirmed to CPJ. Police grabbed 24 News reporter Suhail Mohammed by the neck and forced him into a police vehicle while he was filming. The outlet reported that its video journalist V.S. Rahul was also detained by police, who snatched his camera and threw away the microphone. That evening, police dragged The Caravan’s assistant multimedia producer Ryan Thomas into a detention bus on Janpath Road as he filmed a detention with his press card visible, hit him repeatedly on the head when he refused to delete his footage, slapped him, and prodded him in the stomach with a gun butt in a police car before letting him go at Connaught Place. CPJ has not yet confirmed the names of several other journalists detained on October 11, including a reporter with The Hindu, who was pushed onto a bus and released after mentioning that she was a reporter, as well as a PTI agency journalist . A news agency photojournalist told the media that police dragged them by the neck into a van. Also that day, a group of men wearing press cards surrounded Maktoob Media reporter Fida Fathima, editorial intern Nada Saeeda, and contributor Aktarista Ansari at Connaught Place in the presence of uniformed police. Maktoob Media editor Aslah Kayyalakkath told CPJ the men accused the journalists of insulting Prime Minister Narendra Modi and hurled Islamophobic slurs at them. When Fathima asked the men to show their own press identification, they refused. A senior Delhi Police officer told The Hindu that some journalists may have been detained because they were working close to protesters and did not move away during detention operations. CPJ emailed Delhi Police for comment but did not immediately receive a response. https://cpj.org/2026/10/cpj-demands-isra.body: Share this: Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email Beirut, October 13, 2026 — The Committee to Protect Journalists is deeply alarmed by a recent wave of violations committed by Israeli authorities against the press in Israel and the occupied Palestinian territory. Recent incidents include a local reporter shot with rubber bullets, a Portuguese journalist detained and deported, and the barring of German and British reporters. CPJ demands that Israeli authorities allow the press to operate freely without intimidation or harassment. Israeli forces in the occupied West Bank targeted two journalists documenting the Palestinian olive harvest. On October 8, 2026 , a Portuguese correspondent for the independent outlet Fumaça was arrested in Rantis, northwest of Ramallah, and deported the following day. Ribeiro told CPJ that upon his detention, he identified himself as a journalist, showing his press credentials to the soldiers. He was then taken to a military base where he was threatened with physical assault, and blindfolded. He said that international journalists were removed so that Israeli authorities could continue what he described as an “ethnic cleansing project.” Two days later near Ramallah, Israeli troops fired rubber bullets during clashes involving settlers, striking Palestinian photojournalist Issam al-Rimawi. Al-Rimawi told CPJ that he was wearing an identifiable “Press” vest when the incident occurred. This attack follows similar incidents against Palestinian journalists covering the olive harvest in the West Bank; Israeli settlers attacked Agence France-Presse photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh on October 6, and Israeli authorities detained journalists Mohammad Abed and Mohammad Atiq later that day. On October 11, British journalist Secunder Kermani, working with Channel 4, said he was denied entry into Israel and briefly detained by immigration authorities before the decision was reversed, and he was allowed to enter. Israel also reportedly rejected a work visa application for German journalist Serena Bilanceri, who was set to become Die Tageszeitung’s correspondent there. According to Israeli media , the application was denied due to her “anti-Zionist” views and past reporting calling for sanctions against Israel. Bilanceri told CPJ that the rejection hinders her ability to report from the region. In June, CPJ recorded at least six other cases where journalists were denied entry into Israel, some for expressing opinions critical to the country, and warning of heightened censorship. “Israel’s actions against Palestinian, and foreign journalists are increasing in frequency, demonstrating a clear lack of internal and external accountability,” said Sara Qudah, CPJ regional director. “These repeated incidents of intimidation, detention, deportation, and refusal of entry reveal that Israel continues to operate with complete disregard for international laws preventing retaliation against journalists.” The Israeli Population and Immigration Authority did not immediately respond to CPJ’s request for comment on why the foreign journalists were barred and deported. The Israeli military did not respond toCPJ’s request for comment on the shooting and injury of Issam al-Rimawi.
