https://oceea.osce.org/node/667875.body: Mitigating Climate Change Threats to Critical Energy Infrastructure Story The summer our energy systems hit their limit. What comes next? Date: 1 October 2026 Source: Office of the Co-ordinator of OSCE Economic and Environmental Activities Fields of work: Economic activities , Environmental activities Focus area: Energy security Copied Summer 2026 was the hottest many of us have ever lived through — a season of record temperatures, shrinking rivers, and energy systems pushed to the brink. Across Europe and beyond, extreme heat and drought exposed just how vulnerable critical energy infrastructure has become in a rapidly warming world. In July, water levels on the Danube fell so sharply that long‐submerged WWII wrecks resurfaced near Prahovo, Serbia, preventing regular commercial ship travel. The same low water levels forced Hungary’s Paks nuclear power plant, normally responsible for nearly half of the country’s electricity, to scale back operations because the river could no longer provide sufficient cooling water. Hydropower output across the Alps dropped significantly, with Austria producing only 51% of its usual generation and Switzerland 48%. Serbia’s Djerdap 1 hydropower plant fell to just 20% of capacity. Similar patterns unfolded globally: heatwaves strained grids from California to Jordan, drought reduced reservoir levels across North Africa, and wildfires disrupted transmission lines in multiple regions. These are not isolated incidents, but early signals of a systemic challenge to how billions of people access energy. This reality demands that those responsible for securing our energy future act now, using data, foresight and planning to future‐proof the systems we rely on every day. An unstable energy supply starts with affecting households, but continues with endangering economic stability, environmental safety and national security. When energy systems reach their limits Energy insecurity hits people unevenly. During heatwaves, lower income households struggle to afford cooling, older residents face higher health risks, and families worry about keeping fridges, medical devices, and childcare essentials running during outages. Vulnerable populations are left to endure extreme indoor heat as cooling costs surge. This summer, more than 14,000 people died as a consequence of the heat in Germany – smashing records from previous years. An unstable energy supply starts with affecting households, but continues with endangering economic stability, environmental safety and national security. In a world of interconnected energy systems, disruptions can quickly spill across borders, affecting various markets and grids. The 2026 heatwave is just one example among many of how extreme temperature changes can quickly set off a chain reaction; temperatures that soared above 40°C demanded increased air-conditioning across the board. Drops in river levels decreased hydropower output and limited cooling water for thermal and nuclear plants. Industry slowed down as electricity supply became less stable, and wholesale prices spiked under soaring demand. Emergency protocols needed to be activated across energy infrastructure, underscoring the strain on national security. And the fallout did not stop at borders: cooling‐water constraints in Hungary and Slovakia, for example, meant less available electricity to export and a higher need to import. Supply chains were disrupted across multiple countries, and electricity flow across borders was only possible thanks to regional balancing mechanisms. And while summer’s heat brings its own significant challenges, winters offers little relief. In January 2026, a historic cold snap triggered a gas‐supply crunch across Central Europe, creating a regional energy‐security shock. Households, schools and public facilities struggled with insufficient heating just as prices surged and fuel‐delivery logistics were disrupted by frozen infrastructure and transport delays. What began as a weather event quickly became a multi‐sector crisis, exposing how vulnerable communities and essential services are when our energy systems come under extreme stress. Functioning as an anticipatory risk system, it gives energy decision-makers the ability to look decades ahead and understand how climate trends could reshape the performance, reliability, and security of their energy systems. Preparing for what’s ahead Heatwaves, cold snaps, and severe weather will keep pushing our systems in ways we can’t fully control. But we can reduce how hard those shocks hit us by investing now in stronger grids, diversified energy sources, and smarter planning. Taking action early means our communities, economies, and public services are better protected when the next extreme season arrives. With this in mind, the OSCE built the Energy Security and Risks Platform – an interactive tool that shows where energy systems are most vulnerable to future climate conditions. Functioning as an anticipatory risk system, it gives energy decision-makers the ability to look decades ahead and understand how climate trends could reshape the performance, reliability, and security of their energy systems. The geospatial tool uses a curated sub-set of 60 climate indices to provide high resolution data on future climate risks to existing energy systems, including technologies such as hydropower, solar, wind, thermal, transmission networks and the energy demand side. The platform looks at factors like rising temperatures, changing rainfall, drought, wind patterns, and sunlight, and shows how these changes will affect different types of power plants by the 2050s. It highlights “hotspots” where several problems stack up at once, and where countries may need to have a closer look at their existing infrastructure or rethink long‐term plans. Through the dashboard, decision-makers might be able to answer questions such as “Where will our hydropower systems face drought?” or “Where should we build our next solar panels and wind turbines?” The platform also maps energy‐demand projections. It analyzes how demand is likely to shift under temperature extremes, from increased cooling needs during heatwaves to higher heating requirements during cold spells. A new foundation for energy security Our energy security depends on understanding how the climate will shape the physical limits of our energy systems in the future. To face the challenges that a warming planet is inevitably bringing, we need to be prepared. It will require better planning for grid stability, smarter investment in renewables, strong cross-border co-operation when neighbours face shared risks, and more resilient infrastructure built for the climate of the future. The OSCE’s new platform gives countries the foresight they need to stay ahead of these changes — and to keep the lights on in a warming world. https://www.rferl.org/a/afghanistan-kidn.body: Afghanistan Impoverished Afghans Sell Kidneys On The Black Market 'Out Of Sheer Desperation' By RFE/RL's Radio Azadi October 09, 2026 12:02 CET Impoverished Afghans Sell Kidneys On The Black Market 'Out Of Sheer Desperation' Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Noorudin, an Afghan man, sold his kidney on the black market to feed his family in 2022. Desperate to repay her mounting debts and feed her children, Zahira was forced to make a drastic decision. The mother-of-two from Afghanistan sold one of her kidneys on the black market last year. Even then, the decision did not lift her family out of crushing poverty, and she is now grappling with the health consequences. “I sold my kidney out of sheer desperation,” Zahira told RFE/RL’s Radio Azadi . “We had nothing left, and we were drowning in debt. There was simply no other option. Now, my remaining kidney is starting to fail.” She is not alone. Across the war-torn country of some 40 million people, impoverished Afghans are selling their organs, especially kidneys, to stave off starvation. Most people can survive with just one kidney. The Taliban’s seizure of power in 2021 worsened one of the world’s largest humanitarian crises. Without foreign assistance, the Afghan economy has further shrunk as joblessness and poverty rise. Millions of Afghans rely on food aid, with aid agencies warning of growing malnutrition. Embed share Deep Debt, Failing Health: Afghans Desperate To Escape Poverty Sell Kidneys To Survive by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:02:42 0:00 Some of Afghanistan’s most vulnerable people have resorted to extreme measures to feed their families, including selling organs and, in some cases, their children. Battling To Survive Zahira -- who lives in the western province of Herat and like many Afghans only uses one name -- said she sold her kidney for 100,000 afghanis ($1,550). After paying off part of the family’s debts, she said, “all the money was gone.” The 35-year-old’s husband is elderly and unable to work. Her 16-year-old son crossed illegally into neighboring Iran, where he is trying to find a job. That has left Zahira as the family’s sole breadwinner. “Now it’s just me and my two daughters at home,” said Zahira, who does odd cleaning jobs to pay for their single meal a day. Bismillah, a resident of the neighboring province of Farah, said he tried but failed to sell one of his kidneys. “My options are to sell my child, commit suicide, or steal,” Bismillah told Radio Azadi, adding that he regularly leaves his village to find labor jobs in the provincial capital, Farah city. “I went for five days looking for work and found nothing,” he said. “I’ve been sitting at home for six months. Even if we try to cross into Iran, we just get deported back.” Hundreds of thousands of Afghans have crossed illegally into neighboring Iran to escape extreme poverty and the Taliban’s repressive rule since 2021. But Iran’s ongoing war with the United States and Israel as well as Tehran’s intensifying deportations of undocumented Afghans has left that door increasingly closed to many. SEE ALSO: Afghanistan's Maternal Mortality Crisis Deepens Under Taliban 'One-Kidney Village' Afghans often sell their kidneys through illegal organ-trafficking networks. Local middlemen identify people willing to sell a kidney and match their blood type with buyers, most of them wealthy Afghans or medical tourists from Iran, Pakistan, and the Arab Gulf states. The middlemen often take a substantial share of the proceeds, leaving sellers with only a fraction of the agreed price, according to Sayed Ashraf Sadat, an official in the ousted Western-backed Afghan government who was tasked with investigating the illicit organ trade. Sellers typically receive “only 20 to 30 percent of the actual value of the organ,” said Sadat, adding that the rest is "skimmed off by middlemen and brokers capitalizing on their desperation.” Operations are often carried out in private hospitals or underground clinics, with corrupt medical staff turning a blind eye. In Herat Province, the practice has become so widespread that a settlement was nicknamed “ one-kidney village .” In an apparent response to the booming organ trade in Afghanistan, the Taliban in 2024 banned the sale and purchase of human organs as well as organ transplants. The militant Islamist group said that the transplant of vital organs like the heart, kidneys, and lungs was “un-Islamic.” The move angered patients and doctors, who said thousands of Afghan patients who need transplants for medical reasons would be impacted. Organ transplants are widely used as medical treatment around the world, including in Islamic countries. SEE ALSO: Taliban's Ban On Organ Transplants Deprives Afghans Of Lifesaving Treatment 'No Way To Live' There are no figures for the number of kidneys sold illegally in Afghanistan. But there has been an uptick in reported cases since the Taliban’s takeover, which triggered an economic collapse and worsened an already dire humanitarian disaster. Around 14 million people, or one-in-three Afghans, face acute hunger, according to the United Nations, which said child malnutrition has reached record levels in 12 of Afghanistan’s 34 provinces. The UN World Food Program said in August that conflict, widespread unemployment, soaring food prices, shrinking humanitarian funding, and disruption to supply routes were fueling the hunger crisis. Abdullah, a tribal elder in the northwestern province of Badghis, said locals are selling their organs “out of sheer ruin and poverty.” “May God have mercy and open some door of relief because this is no way to live,” he told Radio Azadi. Gul Ahmad, an elderly father, said he is considering selling one of his son’s kidneys to feed the entire family. “What has this world come to when a man is willing to sell his own son’s kidney and can’t even find a buyer? We are all starving,” he told Radio Azadi. “What choice do I have? There is no aid, no assets, and no work. Where am I supposed to turn?” Written by Frud Bezhan based on reporting by RFE/RL’s Radio Azadi Impoverished Afghans Sell Kidneys On The Black Market 'Out Of Sheer Desperation' Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Follow us Facebook X (Twitter) Youtube Instagram Follow us Print RFE/RL's Radio Azadi RFE/RL's Radio Azadi is one of the

Swathes Of Chernobyl-Affected Land In Belarus To Lose 'Contaminated' Status October 09, 2026 11:43 CET By Amos Chapple and RFE/RL's Belarus Service A 2006 file photo of workers fixing a radiation warning sign near the village of Babchin, Belarus Photo: Vasily Fedosenko (Reuters) Features Too Soon? Swathes Of Chernobyl-Affected Land In Belarus To Lose 'Contaminated' Status October 09, 2026 11:43 CET By Amos Chapple and RFE/RL's Belarus Service Too Soon? Swathes Of Chernobyl-Affected Land In Belarus To Lose 'Contaminated' Status Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google For many Belarusians living in territory contaminated by Chernobyl, the effects of the 1986 nuclear accident will end on January 1, 2027 -- on paper at least. A recent announcement says that 177 cities, towns, and villages will lose their contaminated-area designation at the beginning of 2027, affecting some 566,400 people. A total of 930,600 Belarusians currently live on territory that was contaminated by wind-blown fallout from the nuclear accident in the neighboring Soviet republic of Ukraine. Belarus claimed in August that studies carried out between 2021-2025 showed a “significant improvement in conditions within certain settlements located in radionuclide-contaminated areas." The decision to change the status of the land comes after Belarus's authoritarian leader, Aleksandr Lukashenko, took aim at the designation in an April 2025 meeting . “What have we been doing for 30 years if we have 900,000 people living in contaminated areas?” he said, adding, "the statistics need to be updated.” Belarusians living on contaminated territory today are eligible for significant state benefits , including free meals for students, annual health resort trips for children, and payouts totalling 150 percent of the standard state childcare allowance for some new parents. In the eastern Homel region alone, around 88,000 children living or studying on contaminated land receive state-funded meals each year. Eligible students will reportedly continue to receive free meals up until June 2027. Syarhey Besarab , a Belarusian expert in radiation safety who now lives outside the country, slammed the decision to reclassify the land, which he said will take around another 260 years to return to pre-1986 radiation levels. Besarab points to a complex aftereffect of the Chernobyl disaster in which plutonium-241 that settled on the landscape is transforming into the severely radiotoxic americium-241 as it decays, a process he said will peak in the late 2050s. “Deregulating these lands immediately prior to a secondary surge in extreme alpha radioactivity constitutes a catastrophic failure of prospective safety analysis,” he told RFE/RL. Additionally, he said, some areas within the contaminated land have localized hot spots that “obsolete Soviet macro-evaluation techniques” used by Belarus do not factor in. But not all experts agree on the level of remaining radiation risks. Jim Smith has been studying the fallout from Chernobyl for the past 35 years and was the lead author of a book on the nuclear disaster. The British environmental scientist said in most areas of Belarus and Ukraine today, the risk from radiation is largely limited to foragers and fishermen. “The main pathway for people to ingest radioactivity is from wild foodstuffs -- going out into the forest and eating mushrooms -- if they're eating the berries, if they're catching the fish,” he told RFE/RL. Local authorities in Belarus offer free radiation testing of wild food, and people are warned not to buy mushrooms and berries from roadside stalls. In most urban areas, Smith said, Chernobyl’s radioactive fallout has largely dissipated through a combination of rain and wind, and the short half lives of many of the isotopes released by the disaster. The radiation expert points to cesium-134, which he said, “more or less disappeared in the first 10 years after the accident” due to its two-year half-life. Much of the remaining radioactive material in Belarus today is the longer-lived cesium-137. Outside the highly radioactive exclusion zone on Belarus's border with Ukraine, where people are forbidden to live, Smith said he does not see a significant radiation risk in most contaminated territories. A worker of the Belarusian radiation ecology reserve measures radiation levels in the village of Vorotets in April 2006 In Ukraine, tens of millions of dollars are spent each year on benefits for those affected by the Chernobyl disaster, but Smith predicts Kyiv is unlikely to follow Minsk in reclassifying contaminated land any time soon. “The [Belarusian] government has been much more sort of dictatorial, as you might imagine, saying ‘well, this is what we're going to do regardless.’” In contrast, he said, Ukrainians living in Chernobyl-affected areas “have voted for politicians who don't want to change the status quo.” That perception is shared by Andrey, a Belarusian who was born in the southeast of the country and suffers from a chronic illness he believes is linked to Chernobyl. "The Belarusian authorities don't care about what the people think," the 47-year-old, whose surname has been withheld for security reasons, told RFE/RL’s Belarus Service. "There are no elections, the regime never changes, so they don’t worry about how voters perceive them,” he said, adding, “these benefits were often purely symbolic for people -- you can’t buy a car with them, you can’t build a house. But, still, it was some kind of help.” Smith said the issue of benefits provided to people affected by Chernobyl has proved complex and, in some cases, counterproductive. “It was quite easy to be classified as a victim of Chernobyl, even when the health effect evidence is very difficult,” the environmental scientist said. “Unless you were a firefighter in the plant on the night [of the disaster], for the vast majority of the millions of people that were affected, there's a very low probability that they had a health effect from that, but nevertheless, they were classified as victims of Chernobyl.” A 2002 report by the United Nations Development Program on the aftermath of the disaster highlighted a benefits system that encouraged “potentially harmful or wasteful behaviour.” The report cites people returning to live on contaminated land “in order to be able to claim a higher level of benefits” and others declining to open businesses “for fear of losing Chernobyl entitlements.” But locals in Belarus say there is little chance of any widespread opposition to the upcoming legal change that will have a major impact on many in the authoritarian country. "In Belarus today, it’s dangerous to express outrage about anything," Viktar, who was born in a settlement now in the exclusion zone, told RFE/RL's Belarus Service. The 43-year old, who now lives in the Hrodna region, added that "people just keep their heads down and live their lives." Too Soon? https://www.rferl.org/a/russian-pro-war-.body: Montenegro Head Of Russian Pro-War Blog Detained In Montenegro By Ray Furlong , RFE/RL's Balkan Service and Current Time October 09, 2026 14:07 CET Head Of Russian Pro-War Blog Detained In Montenegro Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Russian military blogger Mikhail Zvinchuk, who runs Rybar, in a photo from April 2023 The head of a leading Russian pro-war blog linked to the country’s Defense Ministry has been detained in Montenegro, along with several other people who work for the publication. Montenegrin Prime Minister Milojko Spajic on October 9 confirmed media reports that Mikhail Zvinchuk, the director of Rybar, and other Russian citizens had been arrested. The blog itself also confirmed the arrests. Zvinchuk is under British and European Union sanctions, with the EU stating that he was in a working group set up by Russian President Vladimir Putin to mobilize support for the war in Ukraine. The US State Department has offered a $10 million reward for information on him and other Rybar figures for seeking to interfere in the 2024 US elections. A US State Department notice calling for information about Zvinchuk and other Rybar figures 'Hybrid Action' “We have been warning that attempts at hybrid action and destabilization relentlessly follow our European path,” wrote Spajic on social media following the arrests. Montenegro applied for membership in the bloc in December 2008, received candidate status in December 2010, and officially opened accession negotiations in June 2012. “The message following today's successful action in which the head of the Rybar information network was apprehended is clear: institutions are doing their job, Montenegro is protecting its interests, and no one will jeopardize our European future,” he added. Montenegrin media outlets reported that five arrests were made in Risan, a small town of some 2,000 inhabitants in the Bay of Kotor -- which has a sizeable Russian expatriate community -- on the country’s Adriatic coastline. The group were filming a documentary criticizing Montenegro’s push for EU membership, they said. A statement on Rybar’s Telegram channel, which has some 1.5 million subscribers in Russian and 80,000 in English, stated that the detained people “were on the country's territory legally and officially.” SEE ALSO: Wider Europe Briefing: Montenegro Edging Closer To The EU It said they were planning to film Cetinje Monastery, an important Serbian Orthodox site that’s about a 90-minute drive from Risan. The statement said Rybar was in touch with Russia’s Foreign Ministry to resolve the situation and “expected all detainees to be released.” Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev, now deputy head of the national-security council, suggested in a social media post arresting Western citizens in Russia to exchange for “our people.” There was no immediate response from Montenegrin security and judicial authorities to RFE/RL’s request for additional details. Some local media are reporting that Zvinchuk’s wife, Valeria, is among those detained. Rybar has become one of the most influential pro-Russian military channels on Telegram since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. In recent years, it has also expanded its activities into the western Balkans, including Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Montenegro has long had fraught relations with Moscow. In 2016, authorities there accused Russia of plotting with a group of Serbian ultranationalists to stage a coup , a charge the Kremlin denied. Ties soured further when the small Adriatic republic joined NATO in 2017. https://www.rferl.org/a/moldova-russia-u.body: Moldova More Drones, More Missiles, No Air Defenses: Moldova In The Cross Fire Of Russia's War On Ukraine By Ionut Benea and Cristina Popusoi October 08, 2026 13:35 CET More Drones, More Missiles, No Air Defenses: Moldova In The Cross Fire Of Russia's War On Ukraine Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Russian drones targeting Ukraine are increasingly crashing onto Moldovan territory, rattling the government, which has limited ability to defend against them. This Gerbera-type drone crashed in northern Moldova last November. CROCMAZ, Moldova -- The watchman was napping in a small hut overlooking a vineyard along Moldova's southeastern border when the afternoon exploded, the earth erupted, and the windows of the outbuilding blew out. The man, who declined to be interviewed, and others in the district flooded local emergency numbers, asking police what was going on. Ion Tabac, an officer with the district border patrol, was one of the responders to the incident on the afternoon of August 9. "We found the trees scorched and destroyed. Smoke was still rising," Tabac told RFE/RL's Moldovan Service. "When the war started in 2022, they weren't flying overhead like this, but lately it happens all the time," he said. Russian drones and missiles zipping through Moldovan airspace is not a new phenomenon for Chisinau. It is, however, something occurring with alarming frequency over the past several months. Moreover, Moldovan authorities say they're tracking a growing number of aerial weapons that are crashing and exploding on Moldovan territory itself. Earlier this week , a border guard was injured when a Russia projectile -- authorities did not say what the object was -- hit the ground near the Palanca crossing along the border with Ukraine and ricocheted. It was the first time a Moldovan law enforcement officer had been injured by a Russian weapon. Russian drones and missiles like this one have flown through Moldovan airspace since the first year of the Russian war on Ukraine. In Crocmaz, what made the crash there even more alarming, officials said, was that the projectile was a new hybrid cruise missile drone called an S-8000 Banderol Despite the uptick in incidents, most Moldovans remain largely apathetic, said Andrei Curararu, a Moldovan political expert. "You can really see splashes of public reaction and fury when something bigger happens. But up to this point, it has been mostly drones exploding in open spaces or with lesser damage. So many people have grown to live with it," said Curararu, who co-founded the Chisinau think tank WatchDog.MD. "It's apathy linked to the fact that it happens. We do not have the capacity to react to it quite concretely," he said. Caught In The Cross Fire Wedged between Romania -- its linguistic and cultural cousin and NATO member -- to the west and war-ravaged Ukraine to the east, Moldova has struggled since the onset of the all-out Russian invasion to minimize the fallout. Since 2022, Russian drones and missile have routinely crossed Moldova airspace en route to Ukrainian targets, usually launched from Black Sea naval ships and installation on the occupied Crimea peninsula. But the increased frequency of both overflights and impacts within Moldova itself has rattled authorities who worry about the possibility of injuries or deaths from Russian weapons. The Defense Ministry says it has recorded nearly 90 "unauthorized incursions" into Moldova airspace, including both drones and missiles. Another Russian Drone Crashed In Northern Moldova by RFE/RL No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:04 0:00 More than half, 48 in total, crashed onto Moldovan soil. The tally included decoys, various loitering strike drones, and missile fragments brought down by Ukrainian air defenses operating close to the border. In August alone, officials recorded 17 incidents where Russian drones crashed or exploded in Moldovan territory, eclipsing the total recorded number for all of 2025. On September 9, a Russian drone hit a crossing along the Moldovan-Ukraine border near Odesa, damaging the border post, sparking a fire, and forcing the evacuation of 16 people. President Maia Sandu wrote in a social media post afterward that Russia's front line is moving further west. A day earlier, a Russian drone over Moldovan airspace prompted authorities to halt flights, including that of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who was flying from Moldova to Norway. "Moscow is putting lives at risk across Europe and must be stopped," she wrote in a post on October 3 after another incident in which she said Banderol missiles and drones "violated our airspace and exploded on our soil." SEE ALSO: Russian Drone Attack Kills 2 Near Moldova As Norway Says Zelenskyy's Plane Nearly Struck While most of the crashes have taken place in rural or unpopulated regions like Crocmaz, several drones have detonated on the outskirts of the capital, Chisinau, rattling sleeping residents. Moldovan authorities are largely helpless against the Russian weapons. The country has two relatively new radar systems, one bought from France and the other donated by the EU, that can detect drones or missiles. Moldova also has some short-range air defenses: mainly so-called MANPADS, shoulder-launched missiles. But it does not have medium- or long-range interception systems capable of shooting down a Russian drone over Ukrainian air space or the Black Sea. "The core problem here is that Moldova doesn't have an effective air defense," Curararu said. "We are in a long line for buying some medium-range defense equipment, but now everything is booked for years and years, and most of it goes to Ukraine." A scorched tree partially damaged by the Russian drone that crashed and exploded near Crocmaz in early August In July, the European Union, of which Moldova is a candidate country, committed 120 million euros toward a medium-range air-defense system for Moldova. But experts say that will take time to acquire and deploy, likely meaning it won't help during the current Russia-Ukraine conflict. Speaking to reporters on September 21, Sandu said the limited air defenses the Moldovan military has at its disposal are deployed to protect critical infrastructure such as the electricity and power grid. "Moldova itself will never do anything as suicidal as going to war with Russia or anything else," Curararu said. "We understand that Moldova is too small to be a factor in this war, anyway. So it could be a collateral victim more than an actor." RFE/RL senior international correspondent Mike Eckel contributed to this report from Prague. https://www.rferl.org/a/dozens-killed-in.body: News Dozens Killed In Russian Strike On Passenger Buses In Kramatorsk By Serhiy Horbatenko and RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service October 08, 2026 13:04 CET Updated October 08, 2026 21:04 CET Dozens Killed In Russian Strike On Passenger Buses In Kramatorsk Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google KRAMATORSK, Ukraine -- Dozens of people were killed in a Russian strike on the Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk on October 8, according to local authorities, a day after another deadly barrage killed at least 25 people across Ukraine. The death toll from the Kramatorsk attack has risen to 33, with 18 others wounded, according to the latest reports from regional authorities and the prosecutor's office. Footage taken by RFE/RL correspondent Serhiy Horbatenko, who visited the site shortly after the attack, showed two buses burned out by the strike, with bodies strewn around the scene. "The bodies are lying right in the middle of the road," the RFE/RL correspondent said while describing the aftermath of the deadly attack. Embed share Russian Strike On Ukrainian Buses Kills More Than 30 Passengers In Kramatorsk by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:28 0:00 The Donetsk Regional Prosecutor's Office said the Russian strike hit two buses that were carrying passengers at the time of the attack. It added that Russian forces likely used guided bombs to strike the vehicles. The strike came a day after at least 25 people nationwide, including two in the capital, Kyiv, were reported killed in the October 7 barrage. In Pryluky, about 150 kilometers east of Kyiv, rescuers searched through the rubble of a destroyed apartment building in northern Ukraine for survivors following a Russian missile attack that killed 22 people, including five children. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it one of the "most vile" attacks in recent memory, and he noted they occurred on the birthday of Russian President Vladimir Putin. Russian forces "destroyed" a residential building "as a birthday 'gift' to Putin," Zelenskyy said in a post to X. At least 10 other such buildings were damaged elsewhere, along with Ukrainian energy infrastructure, one of Moscow's other "key targets," he said. Embed share Massive Russian Attack Kills At Least 22, Devastates Pryluky Apartment Block by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:00:53 0:00 "The fire was right in front of my eyes. There were explosions. I was screaming in my apartment. Extremely scary. I can't describe it," one woman, who gave her name as Lidia, told Current Time at the scene in Pryluky. "So many people have died. I knew everyone here," she added, holding back tears. With a fifth wartime winter approaching, the bombardment was part of near-daily attacks that have steadily increased in frequency and ferocity as the Kremlin struggles on the battlefield front line. Moscow has previously sought to pressure Kyiv into accepting its hard-line demands by attacking the country's energy infrastructure and leaving thousands without heat or electricity amid freezing temperatures. Recently, it has also stepped up attacks on Ukrainian data centers and telecommunications infrastructure, causing Internet outages in some of the country's regions. Since this year, however, Kyiv has increasingly responded to Russian attacks with a campaign of long-range strikes targeting military and energy sites inside Russia and middle-range strikes targeting its key logistics in Ukraine's occupied eastern and southern regions. Embed share Oil Tanker Hit By Naval Drones Near Sochi, Sparking Massive Fire On Black Sea by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:00:53 0:00 Direct link 240p | 1.4MB 360p | 1.9MB 480p | 2.8MB 720p | 4.6MB 1080p | 8.0MB On October 8, Russia's leading AI and technology company, Yandex, said one of its five largest data centers in the Ryazan region had been attacked, adding that the company was trying to restore affected services. The Yandex site hosts tens of thousands of servers. Zelenskyy confirmed Kyiv had struck the facility, saying it was "mirroring" previous Russian attacks on similar sites in Ukraine. Separately, Ukrainian forces also struck the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat oil refinery and petrochemical complex in Bashkortostan, sparking a fire, according to Ukraine's military . Russia's Defense Ministry reported on October 8 that the country's air defenses had intercepted and destroyed 399 Ukrainian drones overnight. SEE ALSO: Exclusive: 'Key Targets': A Russian Blueprint For A Cold, Dark Winter In Ukraine The developments came amid renewed US interest in negotiating a diplomatic settlement to the long-running war. While US President Donald Trump has long said resolving the conflict is one of the key goals of his presidency, Kyiv and Moscow remain far apart in their negotiating positions. Since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, the Kremlin has shown no willingness to compromise on its key demands, including full control over Ukraine's key eastern Donetsk region, which Russian forces have not yet been able to capture. Zelenskyy said Ukraine expected fresh talks with the United States in the coming days, adding that Kyiv hoped its European partners would join the discussions. https://www.rferl.org/a/eu-kosovo-war-cr.body: News EU Says Kosovo's Changes To War Crimes Court Law Violate International Obligations By RFE/RL's Kosovo Service and Gjeraqina Tuhina October 07, 2026 15:34 CET EU Says Kosovo's Changes To War Crimes Court Law Violate International Obligations Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google People celebrate in Pristina after parliament passed legislation limiting the decisions of a Hague-based war crimes court on October 6. The EU has expressed "deep concern" over the amendment. The European Union has expressed "deep concern" over Kosovo's adoption of legislation that seeks to narrow the jurisdiction of a Hague-based war crimes court, saying the changes violate the country's international obligations toward the bloc. The amendments, approved by parliament on October 6, target the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, which last month convicted former President Hashim Thaci and three other former Kosovo Liberation Army leaders of war crimes. In a response to RFE/RL on October 7, an EU spokesperson said the legislation "goes against Kosovo's international obligations toward the EU." "Their current mandate and independence must be fully respected," the spokesperson said. "The Kosovo Specialist Chambers are rendering justice, based on the principle of individual criminal responsibility." Perparim Gruda, a lawmaker from the opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK), which initiated the amendments, rejected the EU's assessment. "I can assure the EU that we are not violating any international obligation with this law," he told a news conference. SEE ALSO: Kosovo Elects President After Opposition Agrees To Last-Minute Deal Gruda said he had not personally seen the EU statement. He cited European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's recent remarks in Pristina, which he characterized as affirming Kosovo's right to amend the law. RFE/RL contacted Kosovo's government about the EU's criticism but had received no response by publication. During the bill's first reading on October 5, Prime Minister Albin Kurti said his Vetevendosje party considered the changes rushed and had little time to analyze them but would support them nonetheless. The Kosovo Specialist Chambers declined to comment directly on the legislation. "The Specialist Chambers is fully focused on implementing its mandate to ensure fair, impartial, and secure judicial proceedings, and to ensure the protection of witnesses and victims," it told RFE/RL on October 7. The amendments' adoption was part of a last-minute agreement between the PDK and Vetevendosje that also paved the way for Justina Shiroka Pula's election as president on October 7. The legislation would restrict the court's jurisdiction to offenses directly linked to organ-trafficking allegations outlined in a 2011 Council of Europe Parliamentary Assembly report. Embed share Police, Protesters Clash In Pristina As Lawmakers Debate Bill On War Crimes Court by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:40 0:00 It would also limit jurisdiction to crimes allegedly committed in Kosovo between July 1, 1999, and December 31, 2000, excluding the earlier period beginning in January 1998. Cases outside that remit would be transferred to Kosovo's regular courts. The amendments also envisage serving sentences in Kosovo and eligibility for presidential pardons. The PDK introduced the initiative five days after the September 16 verdict. Thaci and Jakup Krasniqi each received 25-year sentences, Kadri Veseli 18 years, and Rexhep Selimi 13 years. All four were convicted of war crimes and acquitted of crimes against humanity. Organ-trafficking allegations were not part of their indictment. The verdict is not final, and defense teams have announced appeals. Parliament's approval does not itself overturn those judgments or mean those convicted will be released. SEE ALSO: What Comes Next After The Conviction Of Kosovo's Former President? Gruda also said the final amendment sought to reserve constitutional review of the legislation for Kosovo's Constitutional Court in Pristina, excluding the Specialist Chambers' constitutional chamber in The Hague. Legal experts have warned that changes to the court's mandate could raise constitutional issues and conflict with international obligations. The EU stressed that the court operates within Kosovo's legal system and is enshrined in its constitution. It urged Kosovo to ensure accountability and justice for victims from all communities. In an exchange of letters in April 2014 between Kosovo’s then-president, Atifete Jahjaga, and then-EU foreign policy chief Catherine Ashton, Kosovo made a series of commitments concerning the Specialist Chambers. The exchange formed the basis of the agreement that paved the way for the institution widely known in Kosovo as the Special Court. Among those commitments was an obligation to consult the EU on any proposed legislative changes affecting the court’s mandate or judicial proceedings arising from investigations by the Special Investigative Task Force (SITF). Kosovo also committed to allowing the Specialist Chambers and the Specialist Prosecutor’s Office to continue their work until the relevant investigations and proceedings were completed. Still, the bloc also welcomed Shiroka Pula's election, expressing hope for renewed institutional stability. "While the EU is available to continue supporting Kosovo, our partnership implies not only shared interests but also shared responsibility," the spokesperson said. https://www.rferl.org/a/rubio-athens-ira.body: Iran Rubio In Athens Warns Iran It Will Never Have A Nuclear Weapon By Alex Raufoglu October 07, 2026 13:21 CET Rubio In Athens Warns Iran It Will Never Have A Nuclear Weapon Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google US Secretary of State Marco Rubio (left) speaks during a joint press conference with Greek Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis in Athens on October 7. ATHENS -- US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Iran will never be allowed to acquire a nuclear weapon, declaring that preventing Tehran from doing so is a red line for President Donald Trump. “Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon. Simple, period, end of story,” Rubio said on October 7 in Athens, where he held talks with Greek Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis during the sixth US-Greece Strategic Dialogue. Asked whether Washington was prepared to accept some Iranian uranium enrichment, Rubio declined to specify what level of enrichment might be acceptable. Instead, he said any agreement would have to ensure that Iran “will never have a nuclear weapon.” “That is what our position is. That is the reason why this began,” Rubio said. Rubio also accused Tehran of trying to build such a large conventional military arsenal that it would eventually become difficult for the United States or its allies to act against its nuclear program. “What Iran was trying to do was build up a conventional capability so massive that they would become untouchable,” Rubio said. SEE ALSO: US Sanctions 17 Vessels Linked To Iran's Shadow Fleet He said US military action had severely weakened Iran, including by destroying or degrading much of its drone and missile capabilities and its navy and air force. “They are far less powerful militarily today than they were,” Rubio said. Iran's military capabilities have been significantly degraded during the conflict, although Tehran retains missile and drone capabilities. The current state of its nuclear program remains difficult to assess. with the International Atomic Energy Agency citing limited access for international monitors. Iran Faces 'Freefall' Rubio also portrayed Iran as facing a deepening economic crisis, saying its economy was heading toward “complete freefall.” He pointed to the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the continued flow of oil through the strategic waterway, saying Tehran had lost control of the crucial waterway. SEE ALSO: Iran's Hormuz Leverage Is Fading, But It Isn't Gone While oil shipments have resumed, traffic through the strait remains disrupted and Iran has continued to insist that its full reopening depends on Washington meeting conditions set by Tehran. Rubio blamed Iran's leadership for the country's economic problems, accusing the government of spending its resources on Hezbollah, Hamas, Iraqi militias, and the Houthis rather than improving living conditions at home. “They should have spent their money on their people, and instead they spend the money on terrorism, on weapons,” he said. SEE ALSO: Iran's Medicine Shortages Fuel Black Market For Essential Drugs Rubio said Tehran had previously had multiple opportunities to reach agreements over its nuclear program but had failed to do so. Greece A Key Ally Rubio described Greece as a critical US ally at a time of growing instability in Europe and the Middle East, citing conflicts involving Iran, Russia and Ukraine, and the Red Sea. He called Greece “a source of stability in an unstable world” and praised Athens for increasing defense spending. Greece is on track to meet a commitment to spend 5 percent of its gross domestic product on defense this year, Rubio said, with more than 3.5 percent going toward core defense spending. SEE ALSO: Rubio In Iceland Signals Deeper NATO Push As Russia, China Challenge Arctic Security He also announced that Greece will join the US National Guard's State Partnership Program and be paired with the Florida National Guard, further expanding military cooperation. The two countries also agreed to strengthen cooperation on counterterrorism and information-sharing between law-enforcement agencies. Rubio cited Greece's position on major migration and trafficking routes as making it particularly exposed to terrorism, human trafficking, and transnational crime. Washington and Athens also plan to expand cooperation on US liquefied-natural-gas exports, electricity and gas interconnections, emerging technologies, and regional energy security. The countries are also working together to combat the trafficking of Greek and other Mediterranean antiquities into the United States. Rubio To Make Case For The West Rubio is due to deliver a speech later on October 7 at Athens' Pnyx, overlooking the Acropolis, where he is expected to make a broader argument about democracy, national identity, and the future of the West. According to excerpts of his prepared remarks released by the State Department ahead of the speech, Rubio will call for what he describes as a “great renewal of the Western spirit.” He is expected to argue that ancient Athens embodied qualities that came to define the West, including individual ambition, exploration, invention, competition, and a drive to overcome limits. “Here in Athens, we found the first full realization of all the essential traits that would come to define the West,” Rubio will say, according to the excerpts. He will contrast the ancient Greek pursuit of excellence with what he portrays as a modern emphasis on safety and comfort at the expense of ambition and achievement. “The men who made the Parthenon built upwards,” Rubio is expected to say. 'The Next Decade' Rubio is also expected to portray the West as standing at a historic crossroads. “The next decade will write the story of the next century,” he will say, according to the prepared remarks. He is expected to argue that the United States under Trump has chosen “the unapologetic pursuit of national power,” including rebuilding US manufacturing, strengthening defense, securing critical supply chains, and competing for leadership in emerging technologies. Rubio is also expected to emphasize advanced manufacturing, artificial intelligence, drones, weapons, semiconductors, critical minerals, cybersecurity, energy, and space exploration. His remarks will also challenge the idea that foreign policy should put the interests of a “global community” ahead of a country's own citizens. Rubio is expected to argue that loyalty to one's nation and defending its interests are not selfish, invoking ancient Greek examples of duty, sacrifice, and honor. He will also draw a sharp contrast with Iran's clerical leadership, according to the excerpts, accusing its “radical mullahs” of glorifying death and martyrdom. “Our heroes may be willing to die for their cause; but they do not worship death,” Rubio will say. The speech is expected to cast the confrontation with Iran as part of a wider struggle over the values and future direction of the West, taking Rubio's message in Athens beyond security and diplomacy to a broader defense of national power, Western identity, and democratic traditions. https://www.rferl.org/a/iran-medicine-sh.body: Iran Iran's Medicine Shortages Fuel Black Market For Essential Drugs By Behnaz Jalalipour October 06, 2026 16:20 CET Iran's Medicine Shortages Fuel Black Market For Essential Drugs Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Iranians buy medicines at a pharmacy in Tehran in April. The Iranian Pharmacists Association says around 800 medicines are currently on the country's shortage list. Iran's worsening medicine shortages are pushing patients toward a growing black market, where essential drugs can be found at several times their official prices. The Iranian Pharmacists Association says around 800 medicines are currently on the country's shortage list. The shortages have been compounded by financial constraints, difficulties importing medicines and raw materials, and flight restrictions following the 12-day war with Israel in June 2025 and the ongoing conflict with the United States. Mehdi Pirsalehi, head of Iran's Food and Drug Administration, has cited financial difficulties such as a shortage of the foreign currency needed for imports as a major cause of the crisis. SEE ALSO: 'Just To Survive': Soaring Inflation Puts Iranians' Lives On Hold For patients, the consequences can be severe. A 45-year-old woman being treated for breast cancer told RFE/RL's Radio Farda that pharmacies repeatedly said they were out of stock of the Iranian-version of Aromasin, a drug she must take daily. A 30-tablet pack officially costs 4 million rials (about $1.50). She paid 50 million rials (about $19) on the black market, 12.5 times the official price. She also said she paid at least 30 million rials (about $11) per injection of Zometa, and that two of them turned out to be counterfeit and caused her complications. Like other people who spoke to RFE/RL's Radio Farda, she asked that her name be withheld for security reasons. A 39-year-old man being treated for lung cancer said he now spends 750 million rials (about $279) a month on Sandostatin LAR, which he obtains from pharmacies run by the Iranian Red Crescent Society. Last year, he spent 220 million rials (about $82), marking an increase of 241 percent. According to the Iranian Statistics Center, the average monthly salary in Iran is around $400–500, with wages in cities such as Tehran seen at about double that level. Radio Farda is barred from operating in Iran, and the accounts in this report could not be independently verified. Sold Through Telegram While pharmacies in Iran run short on supplies, Radio Farda found sellers advertising medicines through Telegram groups and other online channels. They were offering drugs for Parkinson's disease, asthma, depression, diabetes and heart conditions. One seller offered RhoGAM, an injection given to Rh-negative women during pregnancy or after miscarriage to prevent complications. The same seller also carried Symbicort, which is prescribed for asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and nortriptyline, which used for depression and migraines. SEE ALSO: Iran Lurching Toward 'Severe Economic Collapse' As War Takes Its Toll Some sellers said flight restrictions imposed because of the war had made it harder to import medicines but that alternative routes remained open. One importer urged buyers to confirm availability first, then offered a long list of medicines for delivery by post. Another seller, a woman, said she worked with her brother, who sources medicines "from wherever he can," while she handles marketing and sales. "You just place the order," she said. "Selling medicine is not profitable at all. We only sell medicine so that we can survive." No Fixed Price Prices on the black market vary widely and often far exceed pharmacy prices. A seller in Isfahan offered Madopar, a Parkinson's drug, for 20 million rials (about $7). At roughly the same time, a seller in Yazd quoted 72 million rials (about $27), more than three times as much. Estradiol valerate, an estrogen medicine, was offered for 40 million rials (about $15), compared with 6 million rials (about $2) at pharmacies. Official prices are climbing, too. A spokesman for the Iranian Pharmacists Association told Iranian media recently that medicine prices had risen by an average of 30 to 70 percent this year. Some foreign-branded drugs had risen by as much as 300 percent. For patients who can find their medicines, the question is increasingly whether they can afford them. For the sellers, as the woman who works with her brother put it, the trade is about getting by. https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/8.body: Listen (2 mins) Save Share Putin pledges Russia’s support to end US-led war on Iran on social media Share Add Al Jazeera on Google Russian President Vladimir Putin, right, and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian pose for a photo on the sidelines of the Commonwealth of Independent States summit in Turkmenistan [Sergei Bobylev/Sputnik/Handout/Kremlin via AP Photo] By AFP and Reuters Published On 8 Oct 2026 8 Oct 2026 Russian President Vladimir Putin has told Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian that Russia will “do everything” to help end the United States-led war on Iran, Russian news agencies reported. The two leaders met in Turkmenistan on Thursday ahead of the summit of the Commonwealth of Independent States, a group of former Soviet nations. “You know our position. On our part, we are ready to do everything we can to help you resolve this situation,” Interfax news agency said Putin told Pezeshkian. “We know that Iran is making real efforts to end the conflict, which broke out through no fault of its own, no fault of Iran’s,” Putin said, according to Russian media. Putin also noted what he called a “positive evolution” in Iran-Russia relations. In a call on Wednesday, Putin told Pezeshkian that Moscow is prepared to mediate efforts to end the war in the Middle East, Iran’s IRNA news agency reported. Putin and Pezeshkian also met on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan last month. Strategic partnership The two countries, which are under heavy Western sanctions, have reinforced diplomatic and military ties. Last year, Moscow and Tehran signed a “comprehensive strategic partnership treaty” that covers areas from trade and military cooperation to science, culture and education. Ukraine and Western countries have accused Iran of supplying Russia with Shahed drones and short-range missiles for use in the Ukraine war. Russia has also been accused of supplying data to Iran for its attacks on US targets in the Middle East. Advertisement The meeting came as Iran-US talks stand at an apparent impasse. US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that the US will not launch an attack on Iran before the November 3 US midterm congressional elections, saying the two countries are holding “productive” talks about ending the ongoing war. Diplomatic efforts to resolve Russia’s offensive in Ukraine also appear deadlocked, even as both sides intensify attacks.

https://www.rferl.org/a/us-ukraine-talks.body: News US, Ukraine Set For Talks In Miami Amid Onslaught Of Russian Air Strikes By Alex Raufoglu October 09, 2026 09:14 CET US, Ukraine Set For Talks In Miami Amid Onslaught Of Russian Air Strikes Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Envoys Jared Kushner (left) and Steve Witkoff (center), who are representing the US in the October 9 talks, meeting with Ukrainain President Volodymyr Zelenskyy (right) in Kyiv on September 6 WASHINGTON -- The US and Ukraine will hold talks in Miami on October 9 to discuss proposals aimed at ending the Ukraine war, amid relentless Russian strikes on vital pieces of infrastructure in Kyiv and other cities ahead of winter. The White House confirmed that envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner would meet Ukrainian representatives on October 9 to discuss a new joint proposal covering all aspects of the conflict and aimed at ending the war. A senior US administration official told RFE/RL that the meeting would provide an opportunity to identify areas where the conflicting sides could cooperate, even where their positions remain different. Previous engagements had produced practical results, including prisoner exchanges, the official said. After the initial meeting, a broader session involving European allies, NATO, and the EU will take place. Rubio Warning The talks follow US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s warning that the conflict has reached a dangerous stalemate, with the risk of escalation beyond Ukraine’s borders. Rubio called the conflict “a very dangerous war” and warned that escalation could include Russian sabotage in neighboring NATO countries, a strike, or other actions that could rapidly widen the conflict. SEE ALSO: Rubio Warns Russia's War Could Spill Beyond Ukraine's Borders That could “quickly turn what is a war between two countries to a much broader, far more dangerous regional conflict,” he said. “In the end, we do not believe that there will be military solutions.... We think this war needs to end, and the negotiated settlement is sooner and better.” US President Donald Trump said this week that he planned to speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin by telephone soon. Sources familiar with the plans said the Miami meeting would focus on proposals that US negotiators had begun developing with Russian and Ukrainian interlocutors during recent visits to the region. The October 9 talks follow several rounds of negotiations held in Florida late last year, including discussions between US officials and Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev in October 2025 and subsequent meetings with Ukrainian officials in November and December that year. Witkoff and Kushner also visited Moscow and Kyiv in early September as Washington renewed efforts to broker an end to the war. They met with Putin in Moscow before holding talks with Zelenskyy and Ukrainian officials in Kyiv. Ukraine is expected to be represented by Kyrylo Budanov, head of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s office; Rustem Umerov, head of Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service and a former defense minister; David Arakhamia, parliamentary leader of Zelenskyy’s Servant of the People party; and Serhiy Kyslytsya, first deputy head of the presidential office. Broader Meeting With NATO, EU A broader meeting involving national-security advisers from the UK, France, and Germany, as well as representatives of NATO, the EU, and US European Command, is scheduled for 11:30 a.m. local time. Talks are expected to resume later at 1:45 p.m. Representatives of the White House National Security Council and the US Treasury Department are also expected to participate. The agenda also includes a postwar prosperity and reconstruction plan for Ukraine and other aspects of a potential settlement, sources said. Zelenskyy said on October 8 that Kyiv’s negotiators had been briefed on the issues to raise with the American delegation, including strengthening Ukraine’s air defenses. “Yes, our negotiators have also been briefed on this for their talks with the American side. They know what to discuss and which pressing issues to raise with the American side,” Zelenskyy told reporters via WhatsApp. SEE ALSO: Dozens Killed In Russian Strike On Passenger Buses In Kramatorsk He added that Ukraine would separately discuss funding and air defense with European partners, including ways to secure financial support more quickly. “Funding issues will be raised there as well -- the details of how to secure the funding sooner. This is very important. And air defense as well,” he said. Zelenskyy said he had also discussed the issues with European Council President Antonio Costa and expressed hope for a positive outcome. John Herbst, who served as US ambassador to Ukraine under President George W. Bush and is now a senior director at the Atlantic Council’s Eurasia Center, told RFE/RL on October 8 that he expected there would be "a good-faith effort by the sides involved,” adding that he did not expect a major confrontation between Washington and Kyiv over the terms of a settlement. Herbst said any serious disagreement between Washington and Kyiv would likely increase Europe’s role in the negotiations, as European governments would be reluctant to see the US put undue pressure on Ukraine to make concessions. Herbst also said the Trump administration wanted to end the conflict and appeared to believe neither side was likely to achieve a decisive military victory. He also cited remarks by Vice President JD Vance suggesting that Ukraine currently has a military advantage. Attacks On Ukrainian Infrastructure In recent weeks, Russia has stepped up its attacks on Ukraine's civilian infrastructure. Schemes, the investigative unit of RFE/RL’s Ukrainian Service, obtained a copy of a Russian-language document from sources in Ukraine’s defense forces outlining a potential blueprint for a campaign by Moscow to inflict enormous suffering on civilians with attacks aimed at sharply cutting supplies of power, heat, and water. Despite Russia’s recent missile and drone attacks, Herbst argued, those strikes were not bringing Moscow closer to winning the war, while Ukrainian operations were making it harder for Russian forces to achieve their objectives. Washington has maintained separate contacts with Russian officials. Russian presidential envoy Dmitriev recently visited Washington for discussions with American officials as diplomatic efforts to end the war continued. https://www.rferl.org/a/iran-russia-targ.body: Iran No Safe Haven: How Iran And Russia Target Exile Enemies By Ray Furlong October 08, 2026 07:10 CET No Safe Haven: How Iran And Russia Target Exile Enemies Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google (illustration) On a Thursday lunchtime in early March, Milad Pourtalebian came home to find his apartment had been broken into and trashed. He then noticed a chilling detail suggesting that this was not a burglary: His "Make Iran Great Again" baseball cap had been skewered to the wall with a large kitchen knife. Pourtalebian is an Iranian citizen who, since arriving in Canada in 2024, has been organizing exile opposition rallies in his adopted hometown of Saskatoon, Saskatchewan. The break-in, days after US and Israeli air strikes launched a war with Iran, followed a series of online threats to the 32-year-old relating to his activities. He immediately reported the incident to local police, telling them he had been targeted for political reasons. Pourtalebian poses with a portrait of Iran's exiled former crown prince, Reza Pahlavi. He says his support of Pahlavi has made him a target. "The incident was initially extremely frightening for me," he told RFE/RL, adding that he has since overcome this feeling. "I decided not to allow fear to stop me from expressing my political views. I think about the thousands of Iranians who have lost their lives seeking freedom." Photos, police documents, and social media screenshots shared by Pourtalebian with RFE/RL give a sense that, despite being thousands of kilometers from Iran, he is not beyond the reach of the country's security services. One Telegram post denounces him for "propaganda activities against the political establishment" and supporting "the attack by America and the Zionist regime against Iran." It concludes by saying, "This person lives in Saskatoon. A few months ago, we tracked him down and conveyed our message to him at his home." This, Pourtalebian said, was "particularly disturbing." Nothing was taken from his apartment, and nobody has been arrested. Transnational Repression Pourtalebian's experience is specific but appears to be part of a wider phenomenon in which authoritarian states pursue their opponents even after they find shelter in apparently safe Western countries. Iran has practiced assassinations and attacks for decades, but its global pressure goes far beyond physical threats. Factnameh, a Persian-language fact-checking service based in Canada, recently noted an increase in "crowdsourced surveillance, doxxing, and cyber-enabled intimidation targeting critics outside Iran." The toolbox includes Alaj, a website where people can make denunciations, that reportedly holds files on some 1,600 people. Iranian state TV threatened those named with "seizure of assets, complete suspension of consular services, and Interpol Red Notices," Factnameh said. Another tool, Goorkan (Persian for "Grave Digger"), publishes personal details of what it calls "traitors." SEE ALSO: Anthropic Disrupts Iran's Use Of Claude To Spread Propaganda, Spy On Dissidents US, British, and Dutch intelligence reported last month that Iran was mounting a global cybercampaign. The FBI said malware named Heavygram was used "to conduct malicious cyber activity to target Iranian dissidents, journalists opposed to Iran, and other opposition groups around the world." Iran is not an outlier in its pursuit of overseas critics. Yana Gorkhovskaia, head of research and analysis at Washington-based Freedom House, has spent years studying the phenomenon. "China, Iran, Russia are among the top 10 perpetrators of transnational repression according to our data. China by far outstrips all other governments," she told RFE/RL. "Of those three, Russia is by far the most violent in terms of assassinations and assaults." Prominent examples include the poisonings of defectors Aleksandr Litvinenko and Sergei Skripal in Britain and a hammer attack on opposition activist Leonid Volkov , an associate of deceased Russian dissident Aleksei Navalny, in Lithuania. 'A Kind Of Paranoia' It is something that's extremely worrying for Mikhail Klimaryov, a Russian cybersecurity expert and Kremlin critic who fled Russia after it launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Embed share 'Psychological War': Exiled Russian Activist Describes How Kremlin Targets Critics Abroad by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:02:21 0:00 Now living in Berlin, where he collaborates with Volkov, the 53-year-old told RFE/RL he detected "a kind of paranoia" in his behavior owing to the threat. "I'm overly concerned about security. At least from the perspective of a normal, healthy person. When I'm out and about, I check whether I'm being followed. Before I touch the door handle to my apartment, I examine it first because there was that case where they smeared a door handle with Novichok," he said. But Klimaryov said his day-to-day life was also affected by a multitude of smaller pressures, ranging from phishing attacks to administrative difficulties, that amount to "a psychological war" waged by Moscow on people like him. He cannot, for example, renew his Russian passport, which expires in 2029. This will impact his residency status in Germany. "It will be an administrative problem, and not as simple as it may seem. I'll need to hire a lawyer," he said. Klimaryov explained he does not have asylum in Germany and does not want to apply for it because this would mean he'd be unable to continue running a business that employs 20 people. Klimaryov insists that despite the Kremlin pressure, he is not a victim. "I'm not in prison. I can earn a living." Travel is another issue. Russia has put him on a terrorist list that can cause a problem at any border. He recalled that while returning from a recent trip to the United States, he was hauled from the boarding line by an officer "with a machine gun and a dog" and questioned for 30 minutes. The danger of extradition means he needs to be careful about which countries he visits. Klimaryov is also listed as a foreign agent in Russia and has debts of some $1 million in fines levied on him by the authorities for, he says, political reasons. In many cases, he was unable to deal with administrative issues mounting against him at home because his Russian phone number was canceled, preventing him from interacting with authorities online or accessing his Russian banking. SEE ALSO: 'Civil Death': The Kremlin Is Building A Legal Purgatory For Exiled Russians Klimaryov says he doesn't use a phone unless required to by German authorities and doesn't give the number to anyone else due to hacking fears. He helps other Russians who come under phishing attacks and says he once almost succumbed to one himself. "I managed to stop myself right at the last moment. It was such a high-level scam," he said, describing a sophisticated back-and-forth exchange of messages with someone posing as a potential client for his company. After weeks of communication, he nearly entered a code delivered by Telegram that could have compromised his account. "Does all this affect me psychologically? Of course it does," Klimaryov said. "I've sought medical advice.... I get hit by panic. Panic attacks -- do you know what those are?" Despite this, Klimaryov insisted he doesn't regard himself as a victim. "I'm better off than many people. I'm not in prison. I can earn a living." But Klimaryov added he is considering medical advice to pause his political activities as a result of the pressure. Gorkhovskaia underlined that this was exactly the point of it. "Surveillance, intimidation, threats to family, digital threats -- they do work, to make people at least second guess whether attending a protest or doing something public is worthwhile," she said. https://www.ozodi.org/a/gurdaamro-furukh.body: Ҷомeа "Гурдаамро фурӯхтам." Бозори "сиёҳ"-и аъзои бадан дар кишвари ҳамсояи Тоҷикистон Октябр 08, 2026 "Гурдаамро фурӯхтам." Бозори "сиёҳ"-и аъзои бадан дар кишвари ҳамсояи Тоҷикистон Ба дигарон фиристед Линкро нусхабардорӣ кунед Facebook X (Twitter) Email Ба дигарон фиристед Ба дигарон фиристед Линкро нусхабардорӣ кунед Facebook X (Twitter) Email Ба дигарон фиристед Бидуни филтршикан Ин пайванд (линк) дар минтақаҳое, ки вебсайти мо бастааст, кор мекунад Мо дар Google "Аз ночорӣ як гурдаамро фурӯхтам. Зери бори қарз монда будам. Дигар илоҷ надоштам. Ҳоло гурдаи дигарам мушкил пайдо кардааст." Зоҳира мегӯяд, гурдаашро ба 100 ҳазор афғонӣ (1550 доллар) фурӯхт Ин нақли Зоҳира, зани 35-сола аз Афғонистон аст, ки соли гузашта барои баргардондани қарзҳои рӯ ба афзоиш ва хӯрондану пӯшондани фарзандонаш яке аз гурдаҳои худро дар бозори “сиёҳ” фурӯхтааст . Аммо Зоҳира мегӯяд, ин тасмими сахт ӯ ва оилаашро аз фақри сангин наҷот надод, баръакс, боиси бад шудани саломатияш гашт. Ин ягона маврид дар Афғонистон нест. Дар саросари ин кишвари ҷангзада, ки ҳудуди 40 миллион аҳолӣ дорад, мардуми муҳтоҷу бенаво барои раҳоӣ аз гуруснагӣ узвҳои бадани худ, бавижа яке аз гурдаҳояшонро мефурӯшанд. Ба дунё чӣ шудааст, ки марде омода аст гурдаи писари худашро бифурӯшад, аммо харидор пайдо карда наметавонад? Ҳамаи мо гуруснаем. Оё интихоби дигаре дорам? На ёрӣ ҳаст, на сармоя ва на кор. Чӣ кор бояд кунам? Ба қудрат расидани гурӯҳи тундрави "Толибон" дар соли 2021 дар Афғонистон вазъи яке аз буҳронҳои бузургтарини башариро дар ҷаҳон бадтар кард. Иқтисоди Афғонистон бе ёриҳои хориҷӣ заиф шуд ва бекориву фақр афзун гашт. Миллионҳо афғонистонӣ муҳтооҷи ёрӣ ҳастанд ва созмонҳои имдодрасон аз афзоиши камғизоӣ дар ин кишвари ҳамсояи Тоҷикистон ҳушдор медиҳанд. Баъзе аз сокинони осебпазиртарин дар Афғонистон барои таъмини аъзои оилаи худ тасмимҳои бисёр сахт мегиранд, аз ҷумла фурӯхтани узвҳои бадан ё дар баъзе маврид фурӯхтани фарзандони худ. Мубориза барои зинда мондан Зоҳира дар вилояти Ҳирот зиндагӣ мекунад ва гурдаашро ба 100 ҳазор афғонӣ (1550 доллар) фурӯхтааст. Ӯ гуфт, пас аз пардохти бахше аз қарзҳои оила "пул тамом шуд". Шавҳари ин зан солхӯрда асту наметавонад кор кунад. Писари 16-солааш ғайриқонунӣ аз марз гузашта, ба Эрони ҳамсоя рафтааст ва дар он ҷо кор ҷустуҷӯ дорад. Дар натиҷа, Зоҳира ягона ноновари хонавода мондааст ва барои таъмини наздикон, аз ҷумла ду духтараш, тамизкорӣ мекунад. Бисмиллоҳ, сокини вилояти Фараҳ, мегӯяд, кӯшиш кард яке аз гурдаҳояшро бифурӯшад, аммо комёб нагашт. "Ман танҳо ин интихобро дорам, ки ё бояд фарзандамро бифурӯшам, ё худкушӣ ва ё дуздӣ кунам," -- гуфт Бисмиллоҳ ба Радиои Озодӣ. Ӯ пайваста барои пайдо кардани кор ба маркази вилоят, шаҳри Фараҳ, меравад: "Чанд рӯз дунболи кор гаштам, аммо наёфтам. Шаш моҳ мешавад, ки дар хона ҳастам. Ҳатто агар кӯшиш кунем, ки ба Эрон гузарем, моро боз ихроҷ мекунанду ба Афғонистон бармегардонанд." Аз соли 2021 садҳо ҳазор афғонистонӣ барои фирор аз фақри шадид ва ҳукумати саркӯбгари "Толибон" ғайриқонунӣ ба Эрон гузаштаанд. Аммо ҷанги идомадори Эрон ва Иёлоти Муттаҳидаву Исроил, инчунин, ихроҷи ҳарчи бештари афғонистониҳо и беҳуҷҷат аз сӯйи Теҳрон ин роҳро барои бисёре аз афғонистониҳо тангтару душворгузар кардааст. Инро ҳам бинед: "Ба танг оварданд, ки қарзро баргардон, гурдаамро фурӯхтам" Деҳае, ки сокинонаш як гурда доранд Афғонистониҳо аксар вақт гурдаҳои худро ба воситаи шабакаҳои ғайриқонунии қочоқи узвҳои бадан мефурӯшанд. Миёнаравҳо аввал касонеро меёбанд, ки омодаанд гурдаи худро фурӯшанд ва гурӯҳи хуни онҳоро бо харидорон месанҷанд. Аксар харидорон афғонистониҳои сарватманд ҳастанд ё аз Эрон, Покистон ва кишварҳои арабии Халиҷи Форс. Саидашраф Содот Саидашраф Содот, як мақоми ҳукумати пешинаи Афғонистон, ки аз ҳимояти Ғарб баҳравар буд ва масъулияти таҳқиқи тиҷорати ғайриқонунии узвҳои баданро ба уҳда дошт, гуфт, миёнаравҳо қисми зиёди пулро мегиранд ва барои фурӯшандагон танҳо як бахши хурди он насиб мекунад. Содот афзуд, фурӯшандагон маъмулан “танҳо аз 20 то 30 дарсади арзиши воқеии узв”-ро мегиранд, дар ҳоле ки “миёнаравҳо ва даллолон бо истифода аз ночории онҳо қисми зиёдро аз худ мекунанд”. Худо раҳм кунад ва ягон роҳи наҷотро бинамояд, чун ин тавр ба зиндагӣ идома додан номумкин аст. Ҷарроҳиҳо одатан дар бемористонҳои хусусӣ ё дармонгоҳҳои пинҳонӣ анҷом мешаванд ва кормандони фасодзадаи тиб ба ин кор чашм мепӯшанд. Дар вилояти Ҳирот ин кор ба ҳадде зиёд шудааст, ки ба як деҳа лақаби “якгурдаҳо" гузоштаанд. Зоҳиран дар посух ба авҷ гирифтани тиҷорати узвҳои бадан дар Афғонистон, ҳукумати “Толибон” соли 2024 хариду фурӯши узвҳои бадани инсон ва ҳамчунин пайванди онҳоро манъ кард. Ин гурӯҳи тундрави исломӣ гуфт, пайванди узвҳои ҳаётан муҳим, аз қабили дил, гурда ва шуш "ғайриисломӣ" аст. Ин тасмим беморону пизишконро дар Афғонистон ба хашм овард. Онҳо гуфтанд, ин иқдом ба ҳазорон беморе, ки дар ҳақиқат бо далели тиббӣ ва барои беҳтар кардани саломати худ ба пайванди узв ниёз доранд, таъсир мерасонад. Пайванди узвҳои бадан дар саросари ҷаҳон, аз ҷумла дар кишварҳои исломӣ, ҳамчун як усули табобат ба таври густурда истифода мешавад. ИНЧУНИН, БИХОНЕД: 700 сокини Тоҷикистон – дар ҷустуҷӯи ҷигари “зинда” "Ин роҳи зистан нест" Дар бораи теъдоди гурдаҳое, ки дар Афғонистон ба таври ғайриқонунӣ фурӯхта шудаанд, омор вуҷуд надорад. Аммо аз замони ба қудрат расидани “Толибон” дар Афғонистон, ки боис ба фурӯпошии иқтисод шуду вазъи оилаҳоро бадтар кард, шумораи мавридҳои гузоришшуда афзоиш ёфтааст. Ба иттилои Созмони Милали Муттаҳид, ҳудуди 14 миллион нафар ё аз ҳар се афғонистонӣ як кас бо гуруснагии шадид рӯ ба рӯ ҳастанд. Ин созмон гуфт, камғизоӣ миёни кӯдакон дастикам дар 12 вилояти Афғонистон ба сатҳи рекордӣ расидааст. Барномаи ҷаҳонии ғизо моҳи август гуфт, даргириҳо, бекории густурда, болоравии босуръати нархи хӯрок, коҳиши кумакҳои башардӯстона ва халалдор шудани роҳҳои таъминот буҳронро дар Афғонистон шиддат мебахшад. Абдуллоҳ, сокини вилояти Бодғис, мегӯяд, мардум узвҳои бадани худро аз нодориву фақри зиёд мефурӯшанд: “Худо раҳм кунад ва ягон роҳи наҷотро бинамояд, чун ин тавр ба зиндагӣ идома додан номумкин аст.” Гул Аҳмад, як марди солхӯрда, гуфт, дар назар дорад барои хӯрондану пӯшондани аъзои хонавода яке аз гурдаҳои писарашро бифурӯшад. "Ба дунё чӣ шудааст, ки марде омода аст гурдаи писари худашро бифурӯшад, аммо харидор пайдо карда наметавонад? Ҳамаи мо гуруснаем. Оё интихоби дигаре дорам? На ёрӣ ҳаст, на сармоя ва на кор. Чӣ кор бояд кунам?" -- гуфт ӯ ба Радиои Озодӣ. "Гурдаамро фурӯхтам."
